query.original_query: in-context learning of novel or unseen languages grammar induction typological distance LLM

sub_queries.semantic_query: mechanistic interpretability of in-context learning for novel languages: grammar induction, typological distance, attention head circuits for language pattern learning in LLMs
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how attention head circuits in large language models implement in-context learning for grammar induction across languages with varying typological distance from English. Using activation patching and causal mediation analysis, we localize knowledge of syntactic pattern generalization to specific attention heads in the middle layers. Our analysis reveals that these heads form distinct functional circuits for word order rules, agreement morphology, and case marking, with circuit reuse decreasing as typological distance increases. We find that the model's ability to learn novel grammatical patterns in-context relies on a shared set of heads that encode abstract positional relationships, rather than language-specific lexical features. Causal tracing experiments show that corrupting these heads disproportionately degrades performance on languages with non-canonical word orders, while leaving noun-verb agreement induction relatively intact. Results further indicate that the residual stream carries compressed representations of grammatical structure, which attention heads read from and write to during few-shot learning. Our findings suggest that in-context learning for grammar induction is mediated by a sparse set of polysemantic attention circuits that generalize across languages through abstract structural features.

sub_queries.semantic_query: human cognitive mechanisms of novel language learning: grammar induction, typological distance effects, statistical learning of unseen languages, cross-linguistic transfer
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the cognitive mechanisms underlying grammar induction in adults exposed to an artificial language with typological features absent from their native language. Participants completed a structured exposure phase followed by a grammaticality judgment task, while we measured behavioral accuracy and reaction times. We manipulated the statistical regularities governing word order and morphological agreement, embedding both consistent and inconsistent patterns. Results indicate that learners successfully extracted abstract grammatical rules, even when those rules conflicted with native-language syntax. However, accuracy was significantly modulated by the typological distance between the artificial language and participants’ first language, with greater distance associated with slower learning curves. Findings support the hypothesis that statistical learning mechanisms operate in concert with prior linguistic knowledge, such that cross-linguistic transfer facilitates acquisition of similar structures but impedes learning of maximally dissimilar patterns. These results are consistent with models of implicit learning that posit a role for both domain-general statistical processes and language-specific biases in novel grammar acquisition.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Understanding and Controlling Repetition Neurons and Induction Heads in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between repetition neurons and induction heads in in-context learning, and how does their ablation affect ICL performance and repetitive generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a layer-wise analysis showing that repetition neurons in late layers are critical for ICL, while middle-layer neurons can be ablated to reduce repetition without harming ICL, and proposes a three-segment ablation strategy for this purpose.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that repetition neurons and induction heads form a cascade for pattern recognition in ICL, and that selective ablation of middle-layer repetition neurons can reduce repetitive generation while preserving ICL performance.
papers.key_findings:
The impact of repetition neuron ablation on ICL performance varies significantly with layer depth.
Repetition neurons in output-side layers serve as critical executors of pattern-based predictions, with effects on ICL performance comparable to induction heads.
Joint ablation of both repetition neurons and induction heads leads to a near-complete breakdown of pattern recognition.
Selectively deactivating repetition neurons in middle layers reduces repetition while preserving ICL performance.
future_direction: Generalizing the three-step pipeline (behavioral pattern detection, neuron/head ranking, targeted ablation) to other problems like memorization.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize repetitive input patterns and their performance on in-context learning (ICL). In contrast to prior work that has primarily focused on attention heads, we examine this relationship from the perspective of skill neurons, specifically repetition neurons. Our experiments reveal that the impact of these neurons on ICL performance varies depending on the depth of the layer in which they reside. By comparing the effects of repetition neurons and induction heads, we further identify strategies for reducing repetitive outputs while maintaining strong ICL capabilities.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: A Theory of Emergent In-Context Learning as Implicit Structure Induction
papers.research_question: When and how does in-context learning (ICL) emerge from generic next-token prediction in language models? The paper investigates the conditions under which ICL capabilities arise from the recombination of compositional operations found in natural language pretraining data.
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical framework showing that in-context learning emerges from next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient compositional structure, and validates this with experiments showing ICL emergence in scaled transformer LMs.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in language models arises from the recombination of compositional structure found in linguistic data, and the paper provides a theoretical and empirical step towards understanding this emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when scaling model parameters and data on compositionally structured pretraining distributions.
Prompting models to output intermediate steps (chain-of-thought) provides a theoretical and empirical benefit over direct prompting.
The success of ICL depends on the complexity of the task's compositional description and the iteration complexity of the pretraining data structure.
Probing experiments indicate that in-context learning is supported by the model learning a representation of the input's compositional structure.
The theoretical bounds are independent of the size of the object universe |Ω|, and empirical performance can even improve with larger |Ω|.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis considers an idealized predictor with infinite data and capacity, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world finite transformer models.
future_direction: Exploring more complex compositional structures and their learnability.
Investigating the application of the theory to real-world natural language data and models.
Extending the analysis to longer chains of reasoning and more complex task compositions.
papers.abstract: Scaling large language models (LLMs) leads to an emergent capacity to learn in-context from example demonstrations. Despite progress, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. We argue that in-context learning relies on recombination of compositional operations found in natural language data. We derive an information-theoretic bound showing how in-context learning abilities arise from generic next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient amounts of compositional structure, under linguistically motivated assumptions. A second bound provides a theoretical justification for the empirical success of prompting LLMs to output intermediate steps towards an answer. To validate theoretical predictions, we introduce a controlled setup for inducing in-context learning; unlike previous approaches, it accounts for the compositional nature of language. Trained transformers can perform in-context learning for a range of tasks, in a manner consistent with the theoretical results. Mirroring real-world LLMs in a miniature setup, in-context learning emerges when scaling parameters and data, and models perform better when prompted to output intermediate steps. Probing shows that in-context learning is supported by a representation of the input's compositional structure. Taken together, these results provide a step towards theoretical understanding of emergent behavior in large language models.

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What are the precise training dynamics during the emergence of induction heads for in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a simple, interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing induction heads and proves that training dynamics are constrained to a low-dimensional subspace, with only three parameters accounting for the emergence.
papers.conclusion: This work shows how induction heads emerge in an ICL task and paves the way for a better theoretical understanding of transformer learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrices of an induction head have a simple structure described by three pseudo-parameters (α3, β2, γ3).
Training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace, and only three dimensions are necessary for the induction head to emerge.
The emergence time of the induction head is quadratic in the context length (Θ(N^2)).
The three parameters emerge in a specific order: γ first, then β, then α.
The emergence of the induction head is self-contained, unaided by the other parameters.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope is limited to a disentangled, attention-only transformer; production models with LayerNorm, MLPs, and additive residual streams may have different dynamics.
Theoretical results assume orthonormal inputs and zero initialization, which may not hold in practice and could alter emergence times.
The study uses a simplified ICL task (exact matching of item-label pairs), not natural language with its complexities.
future_direction: Exploring how data distributional properties like burstiness modulate the effective context length and emergence.
Investigating other means of reducing effective context length, such as special positional embeddings.
Applying a similar approach to study other phenomena like the in-context vs. in-weights learning trade-off, abrupt learning, or other transformer circuits.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant architecture for natural language processing. Part of their success is owed to a remarkable capability known as in-context learning (ICL): they can acquire and apply novel associations solely from their input context, without any updates to their weights. In this work, we study the emergence of induction heads, a previously identified mechanism in two-layer transformers that is particularly important for in-context learning. We uncover a relatively simple and interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing the induction head. We theoretically explain the origin of this structure using a minimal ICL task formulation and a modified transformer architecture. We give a formal proof that the training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace of the parameter space. Empirically, we validate this constraint while observing that only 3 dimensions account for the emergence of an induction head. By further studying the training dynamics inside this 3-dimensional subspace, we find that the time until the emergence of an induction head follows a tight asymptotic bound that is quadratic in the input context length.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that a large fraction of attention heads (~70%) and feed-forward networks (~20%) in a 66B parameter language model can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning performance, and that induction heads (capable of primitive operations) overlap with task-important heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, opening up questions on how to pre-train them to more effectively perform in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 70% of attention heads can be removed with minimal decline in task performance across 14 NLP tasks.
Approximately 20% of feed-forward networks can be removed with minimal decline in task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in intermediate layers, while important FFNs are in later layers.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples.
Induction heads (heads scoring highly on prefix matching and copying) overlap with task-specific important heads, suggesting they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
future_direction: Investigating how to pre-train language models to more effectively perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to perform better with an increase in scale on a wide variety of tasks via the in-context learning paradigm. In this paper, we investigate the hypothesis that the ability of a large language model to in-context learn-perform a task is not uniformly spread across all of its underlying components. Using a 66 billion parameter language model (OPT-66B) across a diverse set of 14 downstream tasks, we find this is indeed the case: $\sim$70% of attention heads and $\sim$20% of feed forward networks can be removed with minimal decline in task performance. We find substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples. We also address our hypothesis through a task-agnostic lens, finding that a small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on their ability to perform primitive induction operations associated with in-context learning, namely, prefix matching and copying. These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, reinforcing arguments by Olsson et al. (arXiv:2209.11895) regarding induction head generality to more sophisticated behaviors associated with in-context learning. Overall, our study provides several insights that indicate large language models may be under-trained for in-context learning and opens up questions on how to pre-train language models to more effectively perform in-context learning.

papers.title: Predicting the Emergence of Induction Heads in Language Model Pretraining
papers.research_question: When exactly do induction heads emerge in language models, and what properties of natural language give rise to induction heads formation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a simple equation combining batch size and context size predicts the emergence point of induction heads, which is agnostic to model size; that bigram repetition frequency and reliability affect IH formation with a Pareto frontier; and that local dependency with high frequency and reliability is sufficient for IH formation, but when these are low, categoriality and marginal distribution shape matter.
papers.conclusion: The emergence of induction heads can be predicted by batch size and context size; frequency and reliability of bigram repetitions define a Pareto frontier for IH formation; and local dependency with high frequency and reliability always leads to IH formation, while categoriality matters only near the frontier.
papers.key_findings:
A simple equation combining batch size and context size predicts the point at which induction heads form, and this emergence point is agnostic to model size.
Surface bigram repetition frequency and reliability strongly affect the formation of induction heads, and there is an effective Pareto frontier in terms of these two values.
Local dependency with high bigram repetition frequency and reliability is sufficient for induction head formation, but when the frequency and reliability are low, categoriality and the shape of the marginal distribution matter.
papers.limitation: Due to limited compute resources, only models up to 350M parameters were trained and up to 7B parameters used for inference, so it is unclear if trends hold for larger models.
future_direction: Extend the study to larger models and other behavioral phases in language model pretraining.
Study the effect of other data properties, such as long-range dependencies, on induction head formation.
Investigate whether the predictive law generalizes to other behavioral phases.
papers.abstract: Specialized attention heads dubbed induction heads (IHs) have been argued to underlie the remarkable in-context learning capabilities of modern language models; yet, a precise characterization of their emergence, especially in the context of language modeling, remains wanting. In this study, we investigate the relationship between statistical properties of the training data and IH formation in both natural and synthetic training data settings. We show that: (1) A simple equation combining batch size and context size predicts the point at which IHs form and that this emergence point is agnostic to model size; (2) Surface bigram repetition frequency and reliability strongly affect the formation of IHs, and we find an effective Pareto frontier in terms of these two values; (3) local dependency with high bigram repetition frequency and reliability is sufficient for IH formation, but when the frequency and reliability are low, categoriality and the shape of the marginal distribution matter.

papers.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
papers.research_question: How does the in-context learning capability emerge in transformers, specifically for learning Markov chains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ICL-MC task as a controlled setting to study in-context learning, showing transformers learn 'statistical induction heads' through phase transitions, and that simplicity bias can delay learning the optimal solution.
papers.conclusion: The ICL-MC task provides a useful controlled setting for understanding in-context learning and the emergence of statistical induction heads, revealing that networks pass through discrete incomplete solutions which may affect the speed of learning more complex circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn statistical induction heads to optimally solve the in-context Markov chain task.
Learning occurs in phases: an initial uniform phase, a unigram phase, and a final bigram phase with a rapid transition between them.
The model's bias towards simpler (unigram) solutions can slow down the learning of the optimal bigram solution.
The alignment between the transformer's layers is crucial for the phase transition to the correct solution.
During training, positional embeddings develop an alternating pattern, with a bias towards looking back an odd number of tokens.
future_direction: Investigate how the presence of simple incomplete solutions affects the formation of more complex circuits in language modeling and other rich learning settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models have the ability to generate text that mimics patterns in their inputs. We introduce a simple Markov Chain sequence modeling task in order to study how this in-context learning (ICL) capability emerges. In our setting, each example is sampled from a Markov chain drawn from a prior distribution over Markov chains. Transformers trained on this task form \emph{statistical induction heads} which compute accurate next-token probabilities given the bigram statistics of the context. During the course of training, models pass through multiple phases: after an initial stage in which predictions are uniform, they learn to sub-optimally predict using in-context single-token statistics (unigrams); then, there is a rapid phase transition to the correct in-context bigram solution. We conduct an empirical and theoretical investigation of this multi-phase process, showing how successful learning results from the interaction between the transformer's layers, and uncovering evidence that the presence of the simpler unigram solution may delay formation of the final bigram solution. We examine how learning is affected by varying the prior distribution over Markov chains, and consider the generalization of our in-context learning of Markov chains (ICL-MC) task to $n$-grams for $n > 2$.

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in language models interact with semantic priors versus input-label mappings, and how does this change with model scale and instruction tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The ability to override semantic priors and learn input-label mappings in-context emerges with model scale, and instruction tuning strengthens both semantic priors and input-label mapping learning, but more so the former.
papers.conclusion: Larger language models do in-context learning differently by being more capable of learning input-label mappings and overriding semantic priors, and instruction tuning further modulates these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Small language models rely heavily on semantic priors and cannot override them when presented with flipped labels in-context.
Large language models can override semantic priors and learn input-label mappings from flipped labels, causing performance to drop below random guessing.
The ability to perform in-context learning with semantically-unrelated labels (SUL-ICL) emerges with model scale, indicating that large models can learn input-label mappings without semantic cues.
Instruction tuning improves the ability to learn input-label mappings in SUL-ICL but also strengthens reliance on semantic priors, making instruction-tuned models less able to override priors with flipped labels.
Large language models can perform linear classification in a SUL-ICL setting, suggesting that the ability to learn input-label mappings extends to non-natural-language tasks.
papers.abstract: We study how in-context learning (ICL) in language models is affected by semantic priors versus input-label mappings. We investigate two setups-ICL with flipped labels and ICL with semantically-unrelated labels-across various model families (GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM, and Flan-PaLM). First, experiments on ICL with flipped labels show that overriding semantic priors is an emergent ability of model scale. While small language models ignore flipped labels presented in-context and thus rely primarily on semantic priors from pretraining, large models can override semantic priors when presented with in-context exemplars that contradict priors, despite the stronger semantic priors that larger models may hold. We next study semantically-unrelated label ICL (SUL-ICL), in which labels are semantically unrelated to their inputs (e.g., foo/bar instead of negative/positive), thereby forcing language models to learn the input-label mappings shown in in-context exemplars in order to perform the task. The ability to do SUL-ICL also emerges primarily with scale, and large-enough language models can even perform linear classification in a SUL-ICL setting. Finally, we evaluate instruction-tuned models and find that instruction tuning strengthens both the use of semantic priors and the capacity to learn input-label mappings, but more of the former.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Localizing Task Recognition and Task Learning in In-Context Learning via Attention Head Analysis
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models mechanistically implement in-context learning, specifically the components of task recognition and task learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in task recognition and task learning, providing a unified mechanistic account of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The TSLA framework successfully localizes TR and TL components to specific attention heads, providing a unified mechanistic explanation of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
TR heads and induction heads are highly overlapping and correlated, indicating that induction heads primarily contribute to task recognition.
TR heads attend more to demonstration labels, while TL heads attend more to query tokens.
Ablating TR heads reduces both accuracy and TR ratio, while ablating TL heads reduces accuracy but not TR ratio.
TR heads align hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label.
The identified TR heads are consistent across tasks, while TL heads are more task-specific.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanistic underpinnings of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models by reconciling two dominant perspectives: the component-level analysis of attention heads and the holistic decomposition of ICL into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL). We propose a novel framework based on Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in TR and TL, and demonstrate their distinct yet complementary roles. Through correlation analysis, ablation studies, and input perturbations, we show that the identified TR and TL heads independently and effectively capture the TR and TL components of ICL. Using steering experiments with geometric analysis of hidden states, we reveal that TR heads promote task recognition by aligning hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label to facilitate prediction. We further show how previous findings on ICL mechanisms, including induction heads and task vectors, can be reconciled with our attention-head-level analysis of the TR-TL decomposition. Our framework thus provides a unified and interpretable account of how large language models execute ICL across diverse tasks and settings.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: Beyond Induction Heads: In-Context Meta Learning Induces Multi-Phase Circuit Emergence
papers.research_question: How is meta-learning ability in in-context learning acquired during training, specifically through the dynamics of the model's internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-learning ability in in-context learning is acquired through multiple phases, each with a distinct circuit emerging, contrasting with the single-phase change observed in induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Multi-phase circuit emergence underlies the acquisition of meta-learning capabilities in in-context learning, and these findings help bridge the gap between controlled mechanistic interpretability experiments and practical large language model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model undergoes three learning phases (Non-Context, Semi-Context, Full-Context) with distinct circuits emerging in each phase.
Sudden jumps in accuracy align with the abrupt emergence of these circuits.
The Semi-Context Circuit explains the random-label robustness phenomenon observed in large language models.
In multi-head settings, circuits emerge in parallel, leading to smoother accuracy improvements while hidden circuit changes still occur.
Similar circuit patterns (chunk example in early layers, label attention in later layers) are observed in pretrained models like GPT2-XL on real-world tasks.
papers.limitation: The work uses a simplified transformer model and synthetic data, which may not fully capture the complexity of real large language model behaviors.
future_direction: Connecting controlled experiments in mechanistic interpretability to realistic use-cases of large language models.
Bridging geometric perspectives (like Local Learning Coefficient) with mechanistic circuit analyses to enrich interpretability methodologies.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit In-Context Learning (ICL), where predictions are made adaptively based on context. While prior work links induction heads to ICL through a sudden jump in accuracy, this can only account for ICL when the answer is included within the context. However, an important property of practical ICL in large language models is the ability to meta-learn how to solve tasks from context, rather than just copying answers from context; how such an ability is obtained during training is largely unexplored. In this paper, we experimentally clarify how such meta-learning ability is acquired by analyzing the dynamics of the model's circuit during training. Specifically, we extend the copy task from previous research into an In-Context Meta Learning setting, where models must infer a task from examples to answer queries. Interestingly, in this setting, we find that there are multiple phases in the process of acquiring such abilities, and that a unique circuit emerges in each phase, contrasting with the single-phases change in induction heads. The emergence of such circuits can be related to several phenomena known in large language models, and our analysis lead to a deeper understanding of the source of the transformer's ICL ability.

papers.title: Unifying Attention Heads and Task Vectors via Hidden State Geometry in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and task vectors jointly shape the hidden state geometry in in-context learning, and can they be unified in a single framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a unified framework linking attention heads and task vectors through the geometry of hidden states in in-context learning, revealing a two-stage mechanism where separability emerges early and alignment develops later.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges the gap between attention heads and task vectors, offering a unified account of the underlying mechanisms of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
ICL improves classification primarily by enhancing the alignment of query hidden states with label unembedding vectors, not by increasing separability.
ICL proceeds as a two-stage process: early layers increase hidden-state separability, while middle-to-late layers improve alignment.
Previous Token Heads (PTHs) drive the early increase in separability.
Induction Heads (IHs) enhance alignment in later layers by amplifying hidden state components along the unembedding directions.
The two-stage phase transition pattern is robust across different ICL settings, models, and extends to generation tasks.
papers.abstract: The unusual properties of in-context learning (ICL) have prompted investigations into the internal mechanisms of large language models. Prior work typically focuses on either special attention heads or task vectors at specific layers, but lacks a unified framework linking these components to the evolution of hidden states across layers that ultimately produce the model's output. In this paper, we propose such a framework for ICL in classification tasks by analyzing two geometric factors that govern performance: the separability and alignment of query hidden states. A fine-grained analysis of layer-wise dynamics reveals a striking two-stage mechanism: separability emerges in early layers, while alignment develops in later layers. Ablation studies further show that Previous Token Heads drive separability, while Induction Heads and task vectors enhance alignment. Our findings thus bridge the gap between attention heads and task vectors, offering a unified account of ICL's underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: Mechanistic Fine-tuning for In-context Learning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently fine-tune language models for in-context learning by directly controlling the attention scores of induction heads, instead of using end-to-end fine-tuning with massive data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), an efficient fine-tuning method for in-context learning that directly optimizes attention scores of induction heads, and shows that this objective is implicit in end-to-end fine-tuning, suggesting a path toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.conclusion: ABFT effectively improves ICL performance by targeting induction heads, and the work demonstrates the potential of controlling model behavior through mechanistic interpretability, opening up the future application of mechanistic controllability.
papers.key_findings:
ABFT significantly improves ICL performance with high efficiency, using only around 0.01% of the data compared to previous methods.
ABFT improves prediction consistency against prompt template and demonstration sampling variations, and reduces bias towards seen labels in unseen-label scenarios.
ABFT is more efficient in time and memory and causes less harm to out-of-domain performance compared to end-to-end fine-tuning.
The ABFT objective is implicitly contained in the end-to-end training objective on ICL-style data, suggesting that such data naturally evokes induction heads.
ABFT demonstrates the possibility of controlling model behavior through intermediate features (attention scores) without supervising the final output, a step toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.limitation:
The induction head-based explanation and ABFT apply only to classification tasks with a finite label set; extending to open-ended tasks remains an open challenge.
The control methods based on gradients and moderate amounts of data are still coarse; future work could focus on gradient-free and data-free model editing.
future_direction: Extending the method to open-ended tasks.
Developing gradient-free and data-free model editing for better mechanistic controllability.
Further improving efficiency by restricting gradient updates to specific transformer layers and automatically optimizing hyperparameters and the induction head filter.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) utilizes structured demonstration-query inputs to induce few-shot learning on Language Models (LMs), which are not originally pre-trained on ICL-style data. To bridge the gap between ICL and pre-training, some approaches fine-tune LMs on large ICL-style datasets by an end-to-end paradigm with massive computational costs. To reduce such costs, in this paper, we propose Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), utilizing the previous findings on the inner mechanism of ICL, building training objectives on the attention scores instead of the final outputs, to force the attention scores to focus on the correct label tokens presented in the context and mitigate attention scores from the wrong label tokens. Our experiments on 9 modern LMs and 8 datasets empirically find that ABFT outperforms in performance, robustness, unbiasedness, and efficiency, with only around 0.01% data cost compared to the previous methods. Moreover, our subsequent analysis finds that the end-to-end training objective contains the ABFT objective, suggesting the implicit bias of ICL-style data to the emergence of induction heads. Our work demonstrates the possibility of controlling specific module sequences within LMs to improve their behavior, opening up the future application of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Secretly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning in GPT models? The paper investigates whether in-context learning can be understood as a form of implicit finetuning.
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning by showing a dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, and provides empirical evidence that ICL behaves similarly to explicit finetuning.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be understood as a process of meta-optimization, specifically as implicit finetuning, and this understanding can inspire improved model designs like momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent.
In-context learning updates attention outputs and weights in a direction similar to explicit finetuning.
In-context learning covers most of the correct predictions made by a finetuned model.
In-context learning and finetuning pay similar attention to training tokens.
A momentum-based attention mechanism, inspired by the dual form, improves performance over vanilla attention in language modeling and ICL tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based architectures and does not cover other architectures like LSTMs.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard Transformer attention may be more complex.
Due to computational cost, the analysis is limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and does not include larger models.
The analysis is based only on classification tasks and does not consider other task types like multiple choice or open-ended generation.
future_direction: Study in-context learning in non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models (e.g., GPT 13B).
Investigate in-context learning on other task types like multiple choice and open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at https://aka.ms/icl.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Why Larger Language Models Do In-context Learning Differently?
papers.research_question: Why do larger language models do in-context learning differently? Specifically, why are larger models more sensitive to noise in the test context compared to smaller models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that smaller models emphasize important hidden features while larger ones cover more hidden features, making smaller models more robust to noise and larger ones more easily distracted during in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the difference in ICL behavior between large and small models is due to larger models covering more hidden features, including noisy ones, making them less robust to noise.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models focus on important hidden features, while larger models cover more features including noisy ones.
Smaller models are more robust to label noise and input noise during ICL evaluation.
Larger models are more easily distracted by noise, leading to worse ICL performance in noisy settings.
Theoretical analysis in linear regression and parity classification settings confirms this behavior difference.
Empirical results on Llama models show that larger models are more sensitive to noise in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not extend to real Transformers easily due to high non-convex function and complicated design of multiple-layer Transformers.
The work does not study optimization trajectory.
The experimental verification uses simple binary classification real-world datasets, which has a gap for practical user using the LLM scenario.
future_direction: Study optimization trajectory of ICL in transformers.
Extend analysis to real Transformers with multiple layers and non-linearities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have emerged as a powerful tool for AI, with the key ability of in-context learning (ICL), where they can perform well on unseen tasks based on a brief series of task examples without necessitating any adjustments to the model parameters. One recent interesting mysterious observation is that models of different scales may have different ICL behaviors: larger models tend to be more sensitive to noise in the test context. This work studies this observation theoretically aiming to improve the understanding of LLM and ICL. We analyze two stylized settings: (1) linear regression with one-layer single-head linear transformers and (2) parity classification with two-layer multiple attention heads transformers (non-linear data and non-linear model). In both settings, we give closed-form optimal solutions and find that smaller models emphasize important hidden features while larger ones cover more hidden features; thus, smaller models are more robust to noise while larger ones are more easily distracted, leading to different ICL behaviors. This sheds light on where transformers pay attention to and how that affects ICL. Preliminary experimental results on large base and chat models provide positive support for our analysis.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning.
