We further present a range of anomalous observations such as a simultaneous phase transition in many tasks coinciding with the learning rate warm-up, and evidence that many context neurons form simultaneously early in training but are later unlearned.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: A Mechanism for Sample-Efficient In-Context Learning for Sparse Retrieval Tasks
papers.research_question: How can transformer models perform in-context learning efficiently, and what are the sample complexity guarantees for such mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a mechanism for in-context learning that includes prompt segmentation and hypothesis learning for sparse retrieval tasks, showing that transformers can implement this mechanism and providing sample complexity guarantees.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that transformers can implement in-context learning mechanisms for sparse retrieval tasks, with theoretical sample complexity guarantees and empirical validation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can segment prompts using maximum likelihood segmentation with sample complexity logarithmic in the number of delimiters.
Transformers can learn a consistent hypothesis for sparse regression tasks with sample complexity O(s log(m/ϵ)/ϵ).
Empirical validation shows that ICL performance depends on delimiter choice and attention maps correspond to theoretical mechanisms.
papers.limitation: The paper does not study the properties of the pre-training process and data distribution, which are crucial for ICL.
future_direction: Expanding the theoretical model to address pre-training process and data distribution
Improving the estimator to use prior probabilities from the base distribution
papers.abstract: We study the phenomenon of \textit{in-context learning} (ICL) exhibited by large language models, where they can adapt to a new learning task, given a handful of labeled examples, without any explicit parameter optimization. Our goal is to explain how a pre-trained transformer model is able to perform ICL under reasonable assumptions on the pre-training process and the downstream tasks. We posit a mechanism whereby a transformer can achieve the following: (a) receive an i.i.d. sequence of examples which have been converted into a prompt using potentially-ambiguous delimiters, (b) correctly segment the prompt into examples and labels, (c) infer from the data a \textit{sparse linear regressor} hypothesis, and finally (d) apply this hypothesis on the given test example and return a predicted label. We establish that this entire procedure is implementable using the transformer mechanism, and we give sample complexity guarantees for this learning framework. Our empirical findings validate the challenge of segmentation, and we show a correspondence between our posited mechanisms and observed attention maps for step (c).

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Unraveling Syntax: How Language Models Learn Context-Free Grammars
papers.research_question: How does language modeling loss decompose with respect to the subgrammar structure of context-free grammars, and do models learn subgrammars in parallel?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language modeling loss decomposes linearly over the subgrammars of a context-free grammar, and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel, unlike children. Subgrammar pretraining can improve performance for tiny models and leads to internal representations that better reflect the grammar's substructure.
papers.conclusion: The work initiates the study of language modeling dynamics with respect to CFG substructure, showing loss decomposes into subgrammar-local contributions and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel. Subgrammar pretraining acts as an inductive bias, and depth of recursion remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Language modeling loss (KL divergence) recurses linearly over the top-level subgrammars of a CFG.
Under certain assumptions, parametrized models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Empirically, small transformers learn all subgrammars in parallel, unlike children who master simpler substructures first.
Subgrammar pretraining can improve final performance for tiny models, and leads to internal representations that better align with the grammar's substructure.
Models struggle with deep recursion, even when they achieve low loss on training data.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical results do not fully explain when gradient-based training yields parallel improvement across subgrammars.
Experiments use a small set of synthetic PCFGs and scaled-down transformers, not covering the full diversity of CFGs (e.g., ambiguous grammars).
It is unresolved whether failures at deep recursion reflect representational limits or optimization barriers.
future_direction: Studying when and why models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Understanding why subgrammar pretraining yields more aligned representations and the optimal pretraining duration.
Exploring the effect of ambiguous CFGs and comparing other language classes in the Chomsky hierarchy.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework for understanding how language models acquire syntax. While large models achieve impressive results, little is known about their learning dynamics. Our approach starts with the observation that most domains of interest, such as natural language syntax, coding languages, arithmetic problems, are captured by probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs). We study the learning dynamics of small models trained on synthetic languages generated from PCFGs, enabling precise control over grammar complexity, recursion depth, and subgrammar structure. We prove several general, recursive formulae for the training loss and Kullback-Leibler divergence over the subgrammar structure of a PCFG. Empirically, we find that unlike children, who first master simple substructures before progressing to more complex constructions, transformers reduce loss across all subgrammars in parallel. We further show that subgrammar pretraining can improve the final loss for smaller models, and that pretrained models develop internal representations more aligned with the grammar's substructure. Finally, we demonstrate that models struggle with deeper recursive structures (a limitation even of large language models), revealing fundamental challenges in how neural networks represent hierarchical syntax. Overall, our work initiates the study of the learning dynamics of transformers on PCFGs as a versatile testbed for probing learning in language models, opening a research direction with many open questions.

papers.title: Learning without training: The implicit dynamics of in-context learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in transformers work? The paper investigates whether the context can be seen as implicit weight updates to the MLP layer.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformer blocks implicitly transform context into low-rank weight updates of the MLP layer, providing a mechanism for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in transformers can be understood as implicit low-rank weight updates to the MLP layer, connecting ICL to model editing and providing a foundation for prompt engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Theorem 2.2 shows that the effect of context on a contextual block corresponds to a rank-1 weight update of the MLP layer.
Proposition 3.1 shows that the implicit weight updates follow a gradient descent-like dynamics as tokens are processed.
Experiments verify that the implicit weight update formula exactly matches the output with context for linear regression tasks.
The implicit weight updates are highly aligned with weight updates from finetuning via gradient descent.
The framework generalizes to other contextual layers like RNNs, but self-attention leads to more stable convergence.
papers.limitation: The implicit weight updates depend on the specific query token, so the context cannot be exactly represented by a single fixed weight update for all inputs.
future_direction: Unifying ICL with model editing by connecting steering vectors and rank-1 edits to the same mechanism.
Developing a formal theory of prompt engineering based on the algebraic properties of the implicit weight updates.
Investigating whether token-dependent updates can be aggregated into static approximations for prompt compression.
papers.abstract: One of the most striking features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their ability to learn in-context. Namely at inference time an LLM is able to learn new patterns without any additional weight update when these patterns are presented in the form of examples in the prompt, even if these patterns were not seen during training. The mechanisms through which this can happen are still largely unknown. In this work, we show that the stacking of a self-attention layer with an MLP, allows the transformer block to implicitly modify the weights of the MLP layer according to the context. We argue through theory and experimentation that this simple mechanism may be the reason why LLMs can learn in-context and not only during training. Specifically, we show how a transformer block implicitly transforms a context into a low-rank weight-update of its MLP layer.

papers.title: Dissecting Multimodal In-Context Learning: Modality Asymmetries and Circuit Dynamics in modern Transformers
papers.research_question: What enables transformers to perform multimodal ICL, both in terms of training data statistics and mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a learning asymmetry in multimodal ICL where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers a learning asymmetry where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE increases the data complexity threshold for ICL emergence.
Multimodal ICL exhibits a learning asymmetry: with high-diversity primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices.
Scaling up unimodal models favors in-weight memorization over ICL, but scaling improves multimodal ICL.
Multimodal ICL relies on induction-style mechanisms that copy labels from matching in-context exemplars.
Encoders improve multimodal ICL by aligning features and providing discriminative representations.
papers.limitation: Observations on production MLLMs are not intended as a mechanistic explanation due to vastly more complex training regimes, data distributions, and architectural choices that confound clean attribution.
future_direction: Investigate circuit-level robustness.
Explore architectural designs that inherently favor robust reasoning over memorization.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based multimodal large language models often exhibit in-context learning (ICL) abilities. Motivated by this phenomenon, we ask: how do transformers learn to associate information across modalities from in-context examples? We investigate this question through controlled experiments on small transformers trained on synthetic classification tasks, enabling precise manipulation of data statistics and model architecture. We begin by revisiting core principles of unimodal ICL in modern transformers. While several prior findings replicate, we find that Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) increases the data complexity threshold for ICL. Extending to the multimodal setting reveals a fundamental learning asymmetry: when pretrained on high-diversity data from a primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices for multimodal ICL to emerge. Mechanistic analysis shows that both settings rely on an induction-style mechanism that copies labels from matching in-context exemplars; multimodal training refines and extends these circuits across modalities. Our findings provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding multimodal ICL in modern transformers and introduce a controlled testbed for future investigation.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Function Induction and Task Generalization: An Interpretability Study with Off-by-One Addition
papers.research_question: What mechanisms inside large language models drive task-level generalization via in-context learning, specifically through the lens of off-by-one addition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'function induction' mechanism in transformer language models that explains how they generalize from seen to unseen tasks via in-context learning, particularly for multi-step tasks like off-by-one addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition is explained by a circuit resembling induction heads but operating at a function level, termed 'function induction'.
The induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads (FI heads) in parallel, each emitting a distinct piece of the function.
The same function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including shifted multiple-choice QA, Caesar cipher, and base-8 addition.
The circuit involves three groups of attention heads: consolidation heads (Group 1), function induction heads (Group 2), and previous token heads (Group 3).
The mechanism is found across multiple models (Gemma-2, Mistral, Llama-2, Llama-3), though with variations.
papers.limitation: The exact role of consolidation heads and why they emerge remains limited, relating to the broader challenge of interpreting 'negative' behavior in language models.
future_direction: Finer-grained interpretation of consolidation heads and their role.
Further investigation into the differences between FI heads and FV heads (function vector heads).
Training toy models to perform off-by-one addition and isolating the circuit requires separate study.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate the intriguing ability to perform unseen tasks via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear what mechanisms inside the model drive such task-level generalization. In this work, we approach this question through the lens of off-by-one addition (i.e., 1+1=3, 2+2=5, 3+3=?), a two-step, counterfactual task with an unexpected +1 function as a second step. Leveraging circuit-style interpretability techniques such as path patching, we analyze the models' internal computations behind their performance and present three key findings. First, we uncover a function induction mechanism that explains the model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition. This mechanism resembles the structure of the induction head mechanism found in prior work and elevates it to a higher level of abstraction. Second, we show that the induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads in parallel, each of which emits a distinct piece of the +1 function. Finally, we find that this function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including synthetic tasks such as shifted multiple-choice QA and algorithmic tasks such as base-8 addition. Overall, our findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: What In-Context Learning “Learns” In-Context: Disentangling Task Recognition and Task Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can we disentangle the contributions of task recognition (applying pre-trained priors) and task learning (acquiring new input-label mappings) from demonstrations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper disentangles in-context learning into task recognition (TR) and task learning (TL), showing that TR is present even in small models but does not scale with model size or demonstrations, while TL is an emergent ability of large models that improves with more demonstrations.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning comprises two distinct phenomena—task recognition and task learning—which emerge under different conditions; future research should distinguish between them and clearly state experimental conditions.
papers.key_findings:
Task recognition (TR) enables non-trivial performance even with randomly labeled demonstrations, but this ability does not improve with larger models or more demonstrations.
Task learning (TL) emerges with model scale; larger models can learn novel input-label mappings from demonstrations, and TL performance consistently improves with more demonstrations.
The performance gap between standard ICL (GOLD) and TR-only (RANDOM) settings increases with model size, indicating TL becomes more significant at scale.
TL generalizes across different types of abstract labels (numbers, letters, symbols), though numbers and letters perform slightly better than symbols.
Task difficulty affects TL scaling; simpler tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis) show steeper TL improvement with scale than harder tasks (e.g., natural language inference).
papers.limitation:
The work is limited to classification tasks because they are easier to adapt to the RANDOM and ABSTRACT experimental setups.
The mechanistic understanding of how task learning actually occurs (e.g., implicit gradient descent vs. mapping to pre-trained concepts) remains elusive.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other types of NLP tasks beyond classification.
Conduct further studies to reveal the mechanistic inner-workings of task recognition and task learning in ICL.
Future work on ICL should clearly distinguish between task recognition and task learning and state the conditions under which experiments are conducted.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exploit in-context learning (ICL) to solve tasks with only a few demonstrations, but its mechanisms are not yet well-understood. Some works suggest that LLMs only recall already learned concepts from pre-training, while others hint that ICL performs implicit learning over demonstrations. We characterize two ways through which ICL leverages demonstrations. Task recognition (TR) captures the extent to which LLMs can recognize a task through demonstrations – even without ground-truth labels – and apply their pre-trained priors, whereas task learning (TL) is the ability to capture new input-label mappings unseen in pre-training. Using a wide range of classification datasets and three LLM families (GPT-3, LLaMA and OPT), we design controlled experiments to disentangle the roles of TR and TL in ICL. We show that (1) models can achieve non-trivial performance with only TR, and TR does not further improve with larger models or more demonstrations; (2) LLMs acquire TL as the model scales, and TL's performance consistently improves with more demonstrations in context. Our findings unravel two different forces behind ICL and we advocate for discriminating them in future ICL research due to their distinct nature.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic Generalization in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the ability of neural language models to make syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure, and how does structural supervision affect learning outcomes and syntactic invariance?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models can learn syntactic generalizations from few examples, and explicit structural supervision improves both few-shot learning and syntactic invariance across transformations.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models are capable of inducing syntactic features from minimal exposure and show some invariance to syntactic transformations, with structural supervision enhancing these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neural models show robust few-shot learning for nominal number and verbal argument structure after minimal exposure.
Structurally supervised models (ActionLSTM and RNNG) outperform the LSTM model in most syntactic generalization tests.
Models demonstrate syntactic invariance by transferring generalizations learned in base contexts to transformed contexts.
There is a singular bias for nouns and a transitive bias for verbs in few-shot learning, with models assuming default categories when evidence is sparse.
Accuracy often improves with increased exposure for some tests, particularly for structurally supervised models.
papers.limitation: The small training data size poses limitations and suggests the need for scaling to larger datasets for better generalization.
future_direction: Scaling the carefully-controlled methods to larger data settings.
papers.abstract: Humans can learn structural properties about a word from minimal experience, and deploy their learned syntactic representations uniformly in different grammatical contexts. We assess the ability of modern neural language models to reproduce this behavior in English and evaluate the effect of structural supervision on learning outcomes. First, we assess few-shot learning capabilities by developing controlled experiments that probe models' syntactic nominal number and verbal argument structure generalizations for tokens seen as few as two times during training. Second, we assess invariance properties of learned representation: the ability of a model to transfer syntactic generalizations from a base context (e.g., a simple declarative active-voice sentence) to a transformed context (e.g., an interrogative sentence). We test four models trained on the same dataset: an n-gram baseline, an LSTM, and two LSTM-variants trained with explicit structural supervision (Dyer et al.,2016; Charniak et al., 2016). We find that in most cases, the neural models are able to induce the proper syntactic generalizations after minimal exposure, often from just two examples during training, and that the two structurally supervised models generalize more accurately than the LSTM model. All neural models are able to leverage information learned in base contexts to drive expectations in transformed contexts, indicating that they have learned some invariance properties of syntax.

papers.title: Task Vectors, Learned Not Extracted: Performance Gains and Mechanistic Insight
papers.research_question: How can we obtain effective task vectors for in-context learning, and what are the mechanisms by which they influence model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which are directly trained and outperform extracted task vectors, and provides a mechanistic analysis showing that task vectors primarily act through attention-head OV circuits and propagate linearly through subsequent layers.
papers.conclusion: LTVs provide an efficient and flexible method for obtaining effective task vectors and offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
LTVs consistently outperform extracted task vectors (Vanilla TV and Function Vector) and match or exceed in-context learning performance across multiple models and tasks.
LTVs are flexible and can be effectively injected at arbitrary layers, token positions, and even into in-context learning prompts.
The low-level mechanism of task vectors involves interaction with attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of 'key heads' being most decisive.
Despite Transformer nonlinearities, the propagation of injected task vectors through subsequent layers is largely linear, characterized by rotation toward task-relevant subspaces in early layers and scaling in magnitude in later layers.
Task vectors exhibit compositionality and cross-task generalization that is constrained by overlap in the label space of tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can perform new tasks from in-context demonstrations, a phenomenon known as in-context learning (ICL). Recent work suggests that these demonstrations are compressed into task vectors (TVs), compact task representations that LLMs exploit for predictions. However, prior studies typically extract TVs from model outputs or hidden states using cumbersome and opaque methods, and they rarely elucidate the mechanisms by which TVs influence computation. In this work, we address both limitations. First, we propose directly training Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which surpass extracted TVs in accuracy and exhibit superior flexibility-acting effectively at arbitrary layers, positions, and even with ICL prompts. Second, through systematic analysis, we investigate the mechanistic role of TVs, showing that at the low level they steer predictions primarily through attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of "key heads" most decisive. At a higher level, we find that despite Transformer nonlinearities, TV propagation is largely linear: early TVs are rotated toward task-relevant subspaces to improve logits of relevant labels, while later TVs are predominantly scaled in magnitude. Taken together, LTVs not only provide a practical approach for obtaining effective TVs but also offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of ICL.

papers.title: Sudden Drops in the Loss: Syntax Acquisition, Phase Transitions, and Simplicity Bias in MLMs
papers.research_question: How does syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerge during training of masked language models, and what is its causal role in the development of grammatical capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerges abruptly during training and is necessary for grammatical capabilities; briefly suppressing SAS early in training can improve model quality by allowing an alternative strategy to emerge.
papers.conclusion: Developmental analysis of training dynamics is crucial for understanding model behavior, and SAS represents a simplicity bias that can be manipulated to improve training.
papers.key_findings:
SAS emerges abruptly during training in a phase transition called the structure onset.
The structure onset precedes and is necessary for the capabilities onset, which marks improvements in grammatical capabilities.
Suppressing SAS throughout training prevents the development of grammatical capabilities.
Briefly suppressing SAS early in training improves model quality and accelerates convergence.
There exists an alternative strategy that competes with SAS, and suppressing SAS allows this alternative strategy to emerge earlier.
papers.abstract: Most interpretability research in NLP focuses on understanding the behavior and features of a fully trained model. However, certain insights into model behavior may only be accessible by observing the trajectory of the training process. We present a case study of syntax acquisition in masked language models (MLMs) that demonstrates how analyzing the evolution of interpretable artifacts throughout training deepens our understanding of emergent behavior. In particular, we study Syntactic Attention Structure (SAS), a naturally emerging property of MLMs wherein specific Transformer heads tend to focus on specific syntactic relations. We identify a brief window in pretraining when models abruptly acquire SAS, concurrent with a steep drop in loss. This breakthrough precipitates the subsequent acquisition of linguistic capabilities. We then examine the causal role of SAS by manipulating SAS during training, and demonstrate that SAS is necessary for the development of grammatical capabilities. We further find that SAS competes with other beneficial traits during training, and that briefly suppressing SAS improves model quality. These findings offer an interpretation of a real-world example of both simplicity bias and breakthrough training dynamics.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Selective Induction Heads: How Transformers Select Causal Structures In Context
papers.research_question: How do transformers select causal structures in context? Specifically, how can they dynamically handle causal structures that change with context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for selective induction heads, showing how transformers can learn to select the correct causal structure in-context for next-token prediction in interleaved Markov chains.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn selective induction heads to dynamically select the correct causal structure in-context.
A 3-layer attention-only transformer can implement the selective induction head mechanism.
The constructed transformer matches the performance of trained transformers.
The mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution.
papers.abstract: Transformers have exhibited exceptional capabilities in sequence modeling tasks, leveraging self-attention and in-context learning. Critical to this success are induction heads, attention circuits that enable copying tokens based on their previous occurrences. In this work, we introduce a novel framework that showcases transformers' ability to dynamically handle causal structures. Existing works rely on Markov Chains to study the formation of induction heads, revealing how transformers capture causal dependencies and learn transition probabilities in-context. However, they rely on a fixed causal structure that fails to capture the complexity of natural languages, where the relationship between tokens dynamically changes with context. To this end, our framework varies the causal structure through interleaved Markov chains with different lags while keeping the transition probabilities fixed. This setting unveils the formation of Selective Induction Heads, a new circuit that endows transformers with the ability to select the correct causal structure in-context. We empirically demonstrate that transformers learn this mechanism to predict the next token by identifying the correct lag and copying the corresponding token from the past. We provide a detailed construction of a 3-layer transformer to implement the selective induction head, and a theoretical analysis proving that this mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution. Our findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Emergence of symbolic abstraction heads for in-context learning in large language models
papers.research_question: How do small transformer models recognize, learn, and generalize abstract sequential symbolic patterns, and do they form internal symbolic representations through abstraction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Small transformer models can learn abstract symbolic patterns and develop abstraction heads for in-context learning, enabling symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Small transformer models can recognize and generalize abstract patterns through abstraction heads, providing insights for neuro-symbolic processing.
papers.key_findings:
Models with 2 or 3 layers successfully solve abstract pattern matching tasks, while 1-layer models fail.
Abstraction heads emerge in attention mechanisms, attending to the first instantiation to generalize patterns.
Variable matching is a simpler task that can be solved even by single-layer models without abstraction.
Training loss shows bumps that correlate with sudden improvements in accuracy, indicating learning of critical strategies.
Abstraction heads operate at a more abstract level than induction heads, focusing on pattern matching from instantiations.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are based on simplified sequences of numbers and may not generalize to human language or complex relations.
The study is limited to small transformer models with 1-3 layers, and different mechanisms may emerge in larger models.
future_direction: Investigate alternative mechanisms for abstract pattern matching in transformers.
Explore the emergence of abstraction heads in larger models with more layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on self-attention circuits are able to perform, at inference time, novel reasoning tasks, but the mechanisms inside the models are currently not fully understood. We assume that LLMs are able to generalize abstract patterns from the input and form an internal symbolic internal representation of the content. In this paper, we study this by analyzing the performance of small LLM models trained with sequences of instantiations of abstract sequential symbolic patterns or templates. It is shown that even a model with two layers is able to learn an abstract template and use it to generate correct output representing the pattern. This can be seen as a form of symbolic inference taking place inside the network. In this paper, we call the emergent mechanism abstraction head. Identifying mechanisms of symbolic reasoning in a neural network can help to find new ways to merge symbolic and neural processing.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Have Attention Heads in BERT Learned Constituency Grammar?
papers.research_question: Do attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa learn constituency grammar, and how does fine-tuning affect this ability?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa partially learn constituency grammar, with higher layers in BERT and middle layers in RoBERTa showing better ability, and fine-tuning with sentence meaning similarity tasks decreases this ability while natural language inference tasks increase it.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa show some constituency grammar ability with layer-specific patterns, fine-tuning affects it differently, and the importance of CGI ability varies between models.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in higher layers of BERT and middle layers of RoBERTa have better constituency grammar inducing (CGI) ability.
Some heads act as a proxy for specific constituency grammar types, but no head fully learns constituency grammar.
Fine-tuning with sentence meaning similarity (SMS) tasks decreases the average CGI ability in upper layers, while natural language inference (NLI) tasks increase it.
For BERT, attention heads with better CGI ability are more important for natural language understanding on QQP and MNLI tasks, but for RoBERTa, this relation is weaker, especially on QQP.
papers.limitation: Attention heads do not fully learn constituency grammar, and it is unclear where syntax information is encoded in BERT.
future_direction: Further study the relations between downstream tasks and the CGI ability in attention heads and explain why different tasks have different effects.
papers.abstract: With the success of pre-trained language models in recent years, more and more researchers focus on opening the "black box" of these models. Following this interest, we carry out a qualitative and quantitative analysis of constituency grammar in attention heads of BERT and RoBERTa. We employ the syntactic distance method to extract implicit constituency grammar from the attention weights of each head. Our results show that there exist heads that can induce some grammar types much better than baselines, suggesting that some heads act as a proxy for constituency grammar. We also analyze how attention heads' constituency grammar inducing (CGI) ability changes after fine-tuning with two kinds of tasks, including sentence meaning similarity (SMS) tasks and natural language inference (NLI) tasks. Our results suggest that SMS tasks decrease the average CGI ability of upper layers, while NLI tasks increase it. Lastly, we investigate the connections between CGI ability and natural language understanding ability on QQP and MNLI tasks.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning via Supportive Pretraining Data
papers.research_question: What makes certain pretraining data supportive for in-context learning, and what are the characteristics of such data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a gradient-based method (ORCA-ICL) to identify a small subset of pretraining data that supports in-context learning and analyzes the characteristics of this supportive data.
papers.conclusion: The work takes a first step towards understanding in-context learning by analyzing instance-level pretraining data, and the findings may guide future pretraining data construction to actively improve models' in-context learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
The supportive pretraining data for in-context learning do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks compared to random pretraining data.
The supportive pretraining data contain a relatively higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens.
The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from incorporating long-range context is below average, indicating that learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages in-context learning.
A continued pretraining on the identified supportive subset significantly improves the model's in-context learning ability, by up to 18%, without improving zero-shot performance.
The cross-task effectiveness of the supportive data suggests that part of the in-context learning behavior is task-specific and not universal across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The supportive pretraining data are identified with respect to the current language model checkpoint, and early checkpoints might have different supportive data.
The ORCA-ICL method is computationally expensive due to its gradient-based nature and the large size of pretraining data.
future_direction: Convert the correlational findings to causal ones to actively refine or construct pretraining data for improved in-context learning.
Apply the ORCA-ICL method to generation tasks in addition to classification tasks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves language models' performance on a variety of NLP tasks by simply demonstrating a handful of examples at inference time. It is not well understood why ICL ability emerges, as the model has never been specifically trained on such demonstrations. Unlike prior work that explores implicit mechanisms behind ICL, we study ICL via investigating the pretraining data. Specifically, we first adapt an iterative, gradient-based approach to find a small subset of pretraining data that supports ICL. We observe that a continued pretraining on this small subset significantly improves the model's ICL ability, by up to 18%. We then compare the supportive subset constrastively with random subsets of pretraining data and discover: (1) The supportive pretraining data to ICL do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks. (2) The supportive pretraining data have a higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens. (3) The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from long-range context is below average, indicating learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages ICL. Our work takes a first step towards understanding ICL via analyzing instance-level pretraining data. Our insights have a potential to enhance the ICL ability of language models by actively guiding the construction of pretraining data in the future.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Generalizations across filler-gap dependencies in neural language models
papers.research_question: Does a neural language model learn a shared representation for filler-gap dependencies across different constructions, or does it rely on superficial properties of the input?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models do not generalize across filler-gap dependencies via a shared representation; they rely on superficial properties of the input and piecemeal learning, indicating a need for linguistic inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: NLMs do not generalize from a shared representation to learn filler-gap dependencies; instead, they rely heavily on input that closely aligns with individual constructions, highlighting the importance of specific linguistic inductive biases for language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
The pretrained RNN shows knowledge of filler-gap dependencies in Wh-movement, clefting, and tough-movement, but not in topicalization.
Augmenting training with clefting examples improves island constraints in clefting and Wh-movement, but not in tough-movement, and fails to generalize to topicalization.
Augmenting with topicalization examples does not lead to full learning of the dependency; the model learns to expect a gap given a filler but not the reverse.
NLMs do not generalize from a shared representation across filler-gap dependencies; they rely on piecemeal learning and input frequency.
The models often fail to capture island constraints fully, especially filled gap effects, and sometimes show reverse patterns relative to grammaticality.
papers.limitation:
Used an RNN architecture rather than a transformer, which may affect generalization capabilities.
Training data is less noisy than child-directed speech, which may not fully simulate language acquisition.
future_direction: Train a smaller Transformer model on the same corpus to determine architectural effects.
Investigate whether increased training time improves syntactic generalization for filler-gap dependencies.
papers.abstract: Humans develop their grammars by making structural generalizations from finite input. We ask how filler-gap dependencies, which share a structural generalization despite diverse surface forms, might arise from the input. We explicitly control the input to a neural language model (NLM) to uncover whether the model posits a shared representation for filler-gap dependencies. We show that while NLMs do have success differentiating grammatical from ungrammatical filler-gap dependencies, they rely on superficial properties of the input, rather than on a shared generalization. Our work highlights the need for specific linguistic inductive biases to model language acquisition.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
Downstream MLP neurons (e.g., neuron 2069 in MLP13) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number direction is language-independent; steering with the English direction flips Spanish predictions.
Similar circuits are found in Gemma 7B and Gemma 2 2B, with analogous attention heads (L22H6 and L19H3) playing the same role.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses solely on Gemma models, which may not generalize to other model families.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), and cannot conclude that the same applies to all other languages, particularly those that are more linguistically distant.
future_direction: Further research could explore whether this pattern holds true for even larger models or across other model families.
papers.abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how universal circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLPs. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. We demonstrate that this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English. Finally, we present evidence of similar behavior in other models within the Gemma 1 and Gemma 2 families.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
