papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Causal Head Gating: A Framework for Interpreting Roles of Attention Heads in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models in a causal manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for causal interpretation of attention heads, and shows that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, head roles are low modularity, and instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: CHG is a flexible and scalable method for identifying causally relevant attention heads, revealing the distributed and context-dependent nature of computation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CHG scores yield causal insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analysis.
LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits.
Individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity).
Instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
CHG does not reveal the precise computations performed by individual heads.
Occasional divergence between G+ and G- scores.
Head roles are context-dependent and vary across runs.
future_direction: Build on these tools to develop circuit-level explanations of how models implement complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: We present causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for interpreting the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models. CHG learns soft gates over heads and assigns them a causal taxonomy - facilitating, interfering, or irrelevant - based on their impact on task performance. Unlike prior approaches in mechanistic interpretability, which are hypothesis-driven and require prompt templates or target labels, CHG applies directly to any dataset using standard next-token prediction. We evaluate CHG across multiple large language models (LLMs) in the Llama 3 model family and diverse tasks, including syntax, commonsense, and mathematical reasoning, and show that CHG scores yield causal, not merely correlational, insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analyses. We also introduce contrastive CHG, a variant that isolates sub-circuits for specific task components. Our findings reveal that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, that individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity), and that instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models learn grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data? What does this consistency reveal about their inductive biases and linguistic representations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, indicating a shared inductive bias. The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional, meaning that overall performance predicts which linguistic generalizations have been acquired.
papers.conclusion: Studying learning trajectories is a promising approach to understand linguistic representations in NLMs, and the consistency suggests a mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2 and TransformerXL) also show similar learning trajectories when aligned by performance level.
The choice of training data has some effect but does not override the consistent ordering.
The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar performance on individual phenomena.
Early in training, NLMs rely on local cues and resemble bag-of-words models; later they become more sensitive to structural cues.
future_direction: Consider the impact of additional factors, architectures and learning phases that appear only later in training.
Develop a theory that can account for the patterns presented by NLMs’ learning trajectories.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
papers.research_question: What enables in-context learning in language models? The paper studies how in-context learning can emerge when pretraining documents have long-range coherence.
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning can be explained as implicit Bayesian inference when pretraining data has long-range coherence, proven in a mixture of HMMs setting and validated with experiments on a synthetic dataset.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be cast as implicit Bayesian inference, providing a first step towards understanding in-context learning and insight for improving pretraining and prompting.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when pretraining documents have long-range coherence and the model infers a latent concept shared across examples.
Theoretical analysis shows that in-context learning error decreases with the number of examples and example length.
Experiments on the synthetic dataset GINC show that both Transformers and LSTMs exhibit in-context learning.
In-context accuracy improves with model scaling despite achieving the same pretraining loss.
In-context learning is sensitive to example order, and zero-shot can sometimes be better than few-shot.
papers.limitation:
The theory assumes the language model fits the pretraining distribution exactly, which may not hold in practice.
The synthetic dataset GINC is simple compared to real-world data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to variable example lengths.
Bridging the mismatch between training and test example lengths.
Analyzing the effect of model scaling and architecture.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LMs) such as GPT-3 have the surprising ability to do in-context learning, where the model learns to do a downstream task simply by conditioning on a prompt consisting of input-output examples. The LM learns from these examples without being explicitly pretrained to learn. Thus, it is unclear what enables in-context learning. In this paper, we study how in-context learning can emerge when pretraining documents have long-range coherence. Here, the LM must infer a latent document-level concept to generate coherent next tokens during pretraining. At test time, in-context learning occurs when the LM also infers a shared latent concept between examples in a prompt. We prove when this occurs despite a distribution mismatch between prompts and pretraining data in a setting where the pretraining distribution is a mixture of HMMs. In contrast to messy large-scale datasets used to train LMs capable of in-context learning, we generate a small-scale synthetic dataset (GINC) where Transformers and LSTMs both exhibit in-context learning. Beyond the theory, experiments on GINC exhibit large-scale real-world phenomena including improved in-context performance with model scaling (despite the same pretraining loss), sensitivity to example order, and instances where zero-shot is better than few-shot in-context learning.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning from Repetitions
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models, and how can it be understood through the lens of surface repetitions and token co-occurrence reinforcement?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel feature-centric perspective on in-context learning by identifying and analyzing token co-occurrence reinforcement, showing how surface patterns both enable and hinder ICL.
papers.conclusion: Token reinforcement is a key mechanism in in-context learning, acting as a double-edged sword that can be leveraged to maximize ICL effectiveness with informed demonstrations.
papers.key_findings:
Token co-occurrence reinforcement exists: the connection between any two tokens strengthens with their contextual co-occurrences.
Token reinforcement helps constrain the output space and enables models to follow patterns like chain-of-thought prompting.
Token reinforcement can lead to spurious connections and cause ICL failures when demonstrations contain unintended patterns.
The reinforcement effect scales with model size, with larger models showing stronger distant reinforcement.
Token reinforcement arises from the model's optimization of training likelihood, as evidenced by empirical analysis of pretraining data.
papers.abstract: This paper explores the elusive mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Our work provides a novel perspective by examining in-context learning via the lens of surface repetitions. We quantitatively investigate the role of surface features in text generation, and empirically establish the existence of \emph{token co-occurrence reinforcement}, a principle that strengthens the relationship between two tokens based on their contextual co-occurrences. By investigating the dual impacts of these features, our research illuminates the internal workings of in-context learning and expounds on the reasons for its failures. This paper provides an essential contribution to the understanding of in-context learning and its potential limitations, providing a fresh perspective on this exciting capability.

papers.title: From Compression to Expression: A Layerwise Analysis of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs extract and differentiate task information from shallow to deep layers during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and analyzes the Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon in ICL, where early layers compress task information from demonstrations and later layers express it for prediction, with implications for performance and robustness.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a comprehensive analysis of ICL internal dynamics, uncovering the prevalent Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon, which deepens understanding of structured representation learning in LLMs and offers practical implications for interpretability, efficiency, and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
The Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon is prevalent across diverse model architectures (transformer and state-space) and task domains (symbolic, language, multimodal).
Larger models and more demonstrations lead to more compressed task representations, explaining performance improvements with scale and context length.
Noisy demonstrations result in less compressed representations, but ICL remains robust up to a certain noise ratio due to distinguishable task vectors.
Attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both bias and variance of task representations as the number of demonstrations increases, as shown in a theoretical analysis.
Task-vector contrastive fine-tuning, motivated by the analysis, can further compress task vectors and improve task-vector accuracy.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis uses a simplified linear attention model, sharing the same simplifications and limitations as prior work on linear self-attention.
future_direction: Theoretical investigation of the phenomenon in the infinite-sample regime.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to adapt to new tasks without weight updates by learning from demonstration sequences. While ICL shows strong empirical performance, its internal representational mechanisms are not yet well understood. In this work, we conduct a statistical geometric analysis of ICL representations to investigate how task-specific information is captured across layers. Our analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon, which we term *Layerwise Compression-Expression*: early layers progressively produce compact and discriminative representations that encode task information from the input demonstrations, while later layers express these representations to incorporate the query and generate the prediction. This phenomenon is observed consistently across diverse tasks and a range of contemporary LLM architectures. We demonstrate that it has important implications for ICL performance -- improving with model size and the number of demonstrations -- and for robustness in the presence of noisy examples. To further understand the effect of the compact task representation, we propose a bias-variance decomposition and provide a theoretical analysis showing how attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both variance and bias, thereby enhancing performance as the number of demonstrations increases. Our findings reveal an intriguing layerwise dynamic in ICL, highlight how structured representations emerge within LLMs, and showcase that analyzing internal representations can facilitate a deeper understanding of model behavior.

papers.title: Re-examining learning linear functions in context
papers.research_question: How do transformers actually perform in-context learning of linear functions? Do they use linear regression or another mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers do not use linear regression for in-context learning of linear functions; instead, they exhibit boundary values determined by training data, leading to a trade-off between precision and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are theoretically capable of learning linear regression for in-context learning, but in practice they do not; instead, they exhibit boundary values that create a dilemma between accuracy and generalizability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention layers are necessary and sufficient for ICL1 of linear functions; MLP-only models fail.
Models have boundary values (B-, B+) that limit generalization, determined by extreme values seen during training.
There is a trade-off: training on restricted intervals yields high accuracy but poor generalization, while training on larger intervals improves generalization but reduces accuracy.
Models do not perform ICL2 (i.e., they do not infer linear function parameters via linear regression).
Models use the entire sequence for prediction, not just a fixed subsequence.
papers.limitation: The proposed hypothesis about how models learn is not fully verified.
future_direction: Probing what models do at various layers to isolate stages of the learning algorithm.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for easily adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to various tasks. However, our understanding of how ICL works remains limited. We explore a simple model of ICL in a controlled setup with synthetic training data to investigate ICL of univariate linear functions. We experiment with a range of GPT-2-like transformer models trained from scratch. Our findings challenge the prevailing narrative that transformers adopt algorithmic approaches like linear regression to learn a linear function in-context. These models fail to generalize beyond their training distribution, highlighting fundamental limitations in their capacity to infer abstract task structures. Our experiments lead us to propose a mathematically precise hypothesis of what the model might be learning.

papers.title: Learning Task Representations from In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How can we develop a task representation that generalizes across modalities like language and mathematical functions, and how can this representation be leveraged to preserve task fidelity on downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated method to encode in-context learning tasks as a weighted sum of attention heads (Learnable Task Vector), which generalizes effectively across text and functional regression modalities.
papers.conclusion: The Learnable Task Vector provides a principled, automated, and modality-agnostic method for representing in-context learning tasks, demonstrating strong generalization across text and regression domains.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Learnable Task Vector (LTV) preserves task information in out-of-distribution (OOD) cases where existing methods fail.
LTV's performance benefits stem from effective task encoding, not from fine-tuning the backbone model.
LTV aligns the distribution of the last hidden state with that of an optimally in-context-learned model, providing insight into task steering.
LTV outperforms existing task vector methods (Function Vector, In-Context Vector) on both regression and language tasks.
LTV requires only a small extension beyond the training sequence length to generalize effectively.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in in-context learning (ICL), where models adapt to new tasks through example-based prompts without requiring parameter updates. However, understanding how tasks are internally encoded and generalized remains a challenge. To address some of the empirical and technical gaps in the literature, we introduce an automated formulation for encoding task information in ICL prompts as a function of attention heads within the transformer architecture. This approach computes a single task vector as a weighted sum of attention heads, with the weights optimized causally via gradient descent. Our findings show that existing methods fail to generalize effectively to modalities beyond text. In response, we also design a benchmark to evaluate whether a task vector can preserve task fidelity in functional regression tasks. The proposed method successfully extracts task-specific information from in-context demonstrations and excels in both text and regression tasks, demonstrating its generalizability across modalities.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning in Transformers and LLMs by Learning to Learn Discrete Functions
papers.research_question: What are the limits of in-context learning in Transformers, is attention necessary, can Transformers exploit teaching sequences for efficiency, and to what extent can LLMs implement learning algorithms from in-context examples?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformers can implement near-optimal learning algorithms for simple Boolean functions, struggle with complex ones like parities, and can adaptively use teaching sequences for sample efficiency. Additionally, pretrained LLMs demonstrate non-trivial in-context learning abilities on discrete tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study advances understanding of in-context learning in Transformers and LLMs, showing their capabilities and limitations on discrete function learning, and highlights the potential for adaptive algorithm selection.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on simple Boolean functions like conjunctions and disjunctions.
Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
Attention-free models such as Hyena perform similarly to Transformers on most tasks, with minor gaps on some.
Transformers can learn from teaching sequences and implement sample-efficient algorithms, adapting based on input.
Pretrained LLMs like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on Boolean function tasks not in their training set.
papers.limitation: Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
papers.abstract: In order to understand the in-context learning phenomenon, recent works have adopted a stylized experimental framework and demonstrated that Transformers can learn gradient-based learning algorithms for various classes of real-valued functions. However, the limitations of Transformers in implementing learning algorithms, and their ability to learn other forms of algorithms are not well understood. Additionally, the degree to which these capabilities are confined to attention-based models is unclear. Furthermore, it remains to be seen whether the insights derived from these stylized settings can be extrapolated to pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs). In this work, we take a step towards answering these questions by demonstrating the following: (a) On a test-bed with a variety of Boolean function classes, we find that Transformers can nearly match the optimal learning algorithm for 'simpler' tasks, while their performance deteriorates on more 'complex' tasks. Additionally, we find that certain attention-free models perform (almost) identically to Transformers on a range of tasks. (b) When provided a teaching sequence, i.e. a set of examples that uniquely identifies a function in a class, we show that Transformers learn more sample-efficiently. Interestingly, our results show that Transformers can learn to implement two distinct algorithms to solve a single task, and can adaptively select the more sample-efficient algorithm depending on the sequence of in-context examples. (c) Lastly, we show that extant LLMs, e.g. LLaMA-2, GPT-4, can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on prediction tasks that are guaranteed to not be in their training set.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: What and How does In-Context Learning Learn? Bayesian Model Averaging, Parameterization, and Generalization
papers.research_question: What type of ICL estimator is learned by large language models? What is a proper performance metric for ICL and what is the error rate? How does the transformer architecture enable ICL?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning (ICL) in perfectly pretrained large language models implicitly implements Bayesian model averaging, and provides theoretical bounds on ICL regret, approximation error, and generalization error.
papers.conclusion: The paper proves that perfectly pretrained LLMs implicitly implement Bayesian model averaging for ICL with O(1/t) regret, shows attention parameterizes BMA, and demonstrates pretraining error decomposes into approximation and generalization errors.
papers.key_findings:
ICL in perfectly pretrained LLMs implements Bayesian model averaging.
The ICL regret is O(1/T) where T is the number of examples in the prompt.
The attention mechanism approximately encodes Bayesian model averaging.
The pretraining error is bounded by an approximation error (decaying exponentially with depth) and a generalization error (decaying sublinearly with dataset size).
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to prompts comprising several examples and does not cover instruction-based prompts.
future_direction: Analysis of instruction-based prompts.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive study of In-Context Learning (ICL) by addressing several open questions: (a) What type of ICL estimator is learned by large language models? (b) What is a proper performance metric for ICL and what is the error rate? (c) How does the transformer architecture enable ICL? To answer these questions, we adopt a Bayesian view and formulate ICL as a problem of predicting the response corresponding to the current covariate, given a number of examples drawn from a latent variable model. To answer (a), we show that, without updating the neural network parameters, ICL implicitly implements the Bayesian model averaging algorithm, which is proven to be approximately parameterized by the attention mechanism. For (b), we analyze the ICL performance from an online learning perspective and establish a $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ regret bound for perfectly pretrained ICL, where $T$ is the number of examples in the prompt. To answer (c), we show that, in addition to encoding Bayesian model averaging via attention, the transformer architecture also enables a fine-grained statistical analysis of pretraining under realistic assumptions. In particular, we prove that the error of pretrained model is bounded by a sum of an approximation error and a generalization error, where the former decays to zero exponentially as the depth grows, and the latter decays to zero sublinearly with the number of tokens in the pretraining dataset. Our results provide a unified understanding of the transformer and its ICL ability with bounds on ICL regret, approximation, and generalization, which deepens our knowledge of these essential aspects of modern language models.

papers.title: Do Attention Heads in BERT Track Syntactic Dependencies?
papers.research_question: Do attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa implicitly capture syntactic dependency relations?
papers.core_contribution: Some attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa specialize in tracking specific syntactic dependency types, but no single head performs holistic parsing well, and fine-tuning has limited impact on attention patterns.
papers.conclusion: Certain specialist attention heads track specific dependency types, but no generalist heads exist for holistic parsing, and fine-tuning does not significantly change attention patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Some attention heads capture dependency types like nsubj and obj with high accuracy compared to baselines.
No attention head forms complete parse trees effectively, as shown by the MST method.
Fine-tuning on MNLI improves accuracy for long-distance clausal dependencies but degrades short-distance ones.
Fine-tuning on CoLA does not significantly affect dependency tracking accuracy.
Attention weights do not fully reflect the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.
papers.limitation:
Analyzing attention weights directly may not reveal much of the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.
Using the gold root in the MST method may artificially improve results, though bias is applied evenly.
papers.abstract: We investigate the extent to which individual attention heads in pretrained transformer language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, implicitly capture syntactic dependency relations. We employ two methods---taking the maximum attention weight and computing the maximum spanning tree---to extract implicit dependency relations from the attention weights of each layer/head, and compare them to the ground-truth Universal Dependency (UD) trees. We show that, for some UD relation types, there exist heads that can recover the dependency type significantly better than baselines on parsed English text, suggesting that some self-attention heads act as a proxy for syntactic structure. We also analyze BERT fine-tuned on two datasets---the syntax-oriented CoLA and the semantics-oriented MNLI---to investigate whether fine-tuning affects the patterns of their self-attention, but we do not observe substantial differences in the overall dependency relations extracted using our methods. Our results suggest that these models have some specialist attention heads that track individual dependency types, but no generalist head that performs holistic parsing significantly better than a trivial baseline, and that analyzing attention weights directly may not reveal much of the syntactic knowledge that BERT-style models are known to learn.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Toward Understanding In-context vs. In-weight Learning
papers.research_question: How do distributional properties of training data affect the emergence and transience of in-context learning (ICL) versus in-weight learning (IWL) in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical and experimental demonstration that in-context learning emerges when training data contains many rare classes (in-context data) and diminishes when sufficient in-weight data is available, explaining the transience of ICL.
papers.conclusion: Simple distributional properties of training data can explain the emergence and eventual disappearance of in-context learning, with ICL and IWL coexisting or dominating depending on the data characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges when there are many rare classes in the training data, as IWL performs poorly on such classes due to insufficient samples.
ICL can become transient when more data is seen, as IWL improves with more samples and eventually outperforms ICL.
The balance between ICL and IWL depends on distributional properties such as the proportion of common vs. rare classes and the relevance of context.
Experiments on synthetic and Omniglot data confirm the theoretical predictions, showing aligned behavior between the simplified model and full transformers.
Fine-tuning a large language model (Gemini Nano) to memorize specific facts reduces its ICL ability, demonstrating that IWL can override ICL.
papers.limitation: The theory does not fully explain the case where ICL and IWL can achieve the same asymptotic performance, leaving open questions about transience in that scenario.
future_direction: Further investigation of the transience of ICL when ICL and IWL have equal performance.
papers.abstract: It has recently been demonstrated empirically that in-context learning emerges in transformers when certain distributional properties are present in the training data, but this ability can also diminish upon further training. We provide a new theoretical understanding of these phenomena by identifying simplified distributional properties that give rise to the emergence and eventual disappearance of in-context learning. We do so by first analyzing a simplified model that uses a gating mechanism to choose between an in-weight and an in-context predictor. Through a combination of a generalization error and regret analysis we identify conditions where in-context and in-weight learning emerge. These theoretical findings are then corroborated experimentally by comparing the behaviour of a full transformer on the simplified distributions to that of the stylized model, demonstrating aligned results. We then extend the study to a full large language model, showing how fine-tuning on various collections of natural language prompts can elicit similar in-context and in-weight learning behaviour.

papers.title: Compositional generalization in a deep seq2seq model by separating syntax and semantics
papers.research_question: Does separating syntactic and semantic processing in a neural machine translation model improve compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel seq2seq model, Syntactic Attention, which separates syntactic and semantic processing streams. This architectural constraint substantially improves compositional generalization on the SCAN dataset without hand-engineered features or additional supervision.
papers.conclusion: Separating syntactic and semantic information processing in neural networks encourages systematic, compositional generalization, drawing a conceptual link to hypothesized brain mechanisms and suggesting a useful heuristic for AI.
papers.key_findings:
The Syntactic Attention model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SCAN dataset's add-jump split, with a median accuracy of 91.0%, a significant improvement over prior models.
The model's performance is highly variable across random initializations on the add-jump split, indicating sensitivity to how the novel verb 'jump' is encoded.
Ablation experiments show that allowing sequential information into the semantic stream ('sequential semantics') degrades compositional generalization, supporting the separation hypothesis.
The model generalizes well from very few examples of a novel verb, achieving near-perfect accuracy with just two training examples containing 'jump'.
The model fails on some SCAN template splits (e.g., 'Primitive opposite right'), indicating limitations in generalizing based on symmetry when training data is skewed.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on the add-jump split is highly variable and skewed across different random initializations, with some runs failing catastrophically.
The separation between syntax and semantics in the brain is likely not as strict as implemented in the model, suggesting the principle may be more of a useful heuristic than a biological fact.
future_direction: Future research should investigate the factors causing performance variability on tasks like the add-jump split and whether other priors or regularization techniques can overcome it.
The principle of separating syntax and semantics may be a useful heuristic in other natural language processing tasks and other systematic or compositional generalization tasks.
papers.abstract: Standard methods in deep learning for natural language processing fail to capture the compositional structure of human language that allows for systematic generalization outside of the training distribution. However, human learners readily generalize in this way, e.g. by applying known grammatical rules to novel words. Inspired by work in neuroscience suggesting separate brain systems for syntactic and semantic processing, we implement a modification to standard approaches in neural machine translation, imposing an analogous separation. The novel model, which we call Syntactic Attention, substantially outperforms standard methods in deep learning on the SCAN dataset, a compositional generalization task, without any hand-engineered features or additional supervision. Our work suggests that separating syntactic from semantic learning may be a useful heuristic for capturing compositional structure.

papers.title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is in-context learning (ICL) in transformers a persistent phenomenon, or does it emerge and then disappear (become transient) during training?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning (ICL) in transformers is often transient: it emerges and then disappears during training, even as training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for in-weights learning (IWL).
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is often transient, emphasizing the importance of validation metrics, early stopping, or regularization to preserve ICL capabilities during training.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges and then disappears (is transient) during training, while IWL accuracy increases.
ICL transience occurs across a range of model sizes (depth, embedding dimension), dataset sizes (number of classes, exemplars per class), and dataset types (Omniglot images, LLaMa token embeddings).
Data distributional properties, such as a larger number of classes or a Zipfian skew, can postpone the transience of ICL.
L2 regularization can mitigate or eliminate ICL transience, potentially by favoring the lower-norm ICL circuit.
Preliminary evidence suggests ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits for resources in the transformer's residual stream.
future_direction: Explore the effect of alternate optimizers or initialization schemes on the transience of ICL.
Connect findings to natural language settings and large-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks can exhibit a surprising capacity for in-context learning (ICL) despite not being explicitly trained for it. Prior work has provided a deeper understanding of how ICL emerges in transformers, e.g. through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, Bayesian inference, or by examining the distributional properties of training data. However, in each of these cases, ICL is treated largely as a persistent phenomenon; namely, once ICL emerges, it is assumed to persist asymptotically. Here, we show that the emergence of ICL during transformer training is, in fact, often transient. We train transformers on synthetic data designed so that both ICL and in-weights learning (IWL) strategies can lead to correct predictions. We find that ICL first emerges, then disappears and gives way to IWL, all while the training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for IWL. The transient nature of ICL is observed in transformers across a range of model sizes and datasets, raising the question of how much to "overtrain" transformers when seeking compact, cheaper-to-run models. We find that L2 regularization may offer a path to more persistent ICL that removes the need for early stopping based on ICL-style validation tasks. Finally, we present initial evidence that ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in a transformer language model differentiate and specialize during training, as revealed by refined local learning coefficients?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces refined local learning coefficients (rLLCs) as a principled, quantitative toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing how attention heads differentiate and specialize during training and enabling the discovery of a novel multigram circuit.
papers.conclusion: Refined local learning coefficients provide a powerful toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing the interplay between data distributional structure, loss landscape geometry, learning dynamics, and the resulting computational structure in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-refined LLCs (wrLLCs) reveal how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional types (e.g., induction heads, multigram heads) over the course of training.
Data-refined LLCs (drLLCs) show how heads specialize to different data distributions, such as one induction head specializing more to code.
The combination of refined LLCs leads to the identification of a novel multigram circuit involving coordination between layer 0 and layer 1 multigram heads.
The developmental perspective (evolution over time) is crucial for understanding the emergence of internal structure; point estimates at the end of training are insufficient.
Refined LLCs provide a quantitative link between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures.
papers.limitation:
The justification of the LLC estimator presumes that w* is a local minima of the population loss, but there is no clear way to ascertain this in practice, and estimates are often performed during training where this is unlikely.
The ground truth LLC is unknown, so the accuracy of estimated LLC values cannot be guaranteed, though there is reason to believe the ordinality is correct.
future_direction: Establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: We introduce refined variants of the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC), a measure of model complexity grounded in singular learning theory, to study the development of internal structure in transformer language models during training. By applying these \textit{refined LLCs} (rLLCs) to individual components of a two-layer attention-only transformer, we gain novel insights into the progressive differentiation and specialization of attention heads. Our methodology reveals how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional roles over the course of training, analyzes the types of data these heads specialize to process, and discovers a previously unidentified multigram circuit. These findings demonstrate that rLLCs provide a principled, quantitative toolkit for \textit{developmental interpretability}, which aims to understand models through their evolution across the learning process. More broadly, this work takes a step towards establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.

papers.title: Theoretical Understanding of In-Context Learning in Shallow Transformers with Unstructured Data
papers.research_question: How can transformers learn from unstructured data (where input and output are in separate tokens) in in-context learning, and what roles do components like attention layers, attention mask, and positional encoding play?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a two-layer transformer with a look-ahead attention mask is necessary to learn from unstructured data in ICL, and that positional encoding improves performance by matching input and output tokens.
papers.conclusion: Two attention layers and an attention mask are crucial for learning from unstructured data in ICL, and positional encoding further enhances performance by facilitating token matching.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer transformer fails to learn from unstructured data in ICL.
A two-layer transformer with a look-ahead attention mask can successfully learn from unstructured data.
Positional encoding helps match input and output tokens, improving ICL performance.
A larger embedding dimension allows the model to handle more in-context examples.
papers.limitation: The paper only considers a simple transformer architecture, which may not capture the full characteristics of transformers used in real practice.
future_direction: Analyzing the effect of using softmax attention in the second layer.
Studying the effect of having more than two attention layers.
Investigating the effect of positional encoding on training dynamics and generalization.
Extending the analysis to chain-of-thought.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful models that can learn concepts at the inference stage via in-context learning (ICL). While theoretical studies, e.g., \cite{zhang2023trained}, attempt to explain the mechanism of ICL, they assume the input $x_i$ and the output $y_i$ of each demonstration example are in the same token (i.e., structured data). However, in real practice, the examples are usually text input, and all words, regardless of their logic relationship, are stored in different tokens (i.e., unstructured data \cite{wibisono2023role}). To understand how LLMs learn from the unstructured data in ICL, this paper studies the role of each component in the transformer architecture and provides a theoretical understanding to explain the success of the architecture. In particular, we consider a simple transformer with one/two attention layers and linear regression tasks for the ICL prediction. We observe that (1) a transformer with two layers of (self-)attentions with a look-ahead attention mask can learn from the prompt in the unstructured data, and (2) positional encoding can match the $x_i$ and $y_i$ tokens to achieve a better ICL performance.

papers.title: Provable Low-Frequency Bias of In-Context Learning of Representations
papers.research_question: How does the double convergence process in in-context learning lead to an implicit bias towards smooth (low-frequency) representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the double convergence framework to explain the low-frequency bias in in-context learning, providing theoretical explanations for several empirical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: The double convergence phenomenon leads to a low-frequency bias in in-context learning, explaining several observed phenomena and providing a theoretical foundation for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Double convergence (context-wise and layer-wise) leads to an implicit low-frequency bias in hidden representations.
Explains why in-context learning can suppress the original semantic meaning learned during pre-training.
Explains why learned representations form a globally structured but locally distorted geometry.
Explains why the energy of representations decays but does not converge to zero.
Predicts and empirically verifies that in-context learning exhibits intrinsic robustness to high-frequency noise in the input.
papers.limitation: The most detailed results focus on the specific data-generating process (random walk on a graph) from Park et al. (2024), and generalizing to broader data distributions remains an open direction.
future_direction: Generalizing the analysis to broader data distributions.
Analyzing how the structural assumptions on attention maps emerge from pre-training.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to acquire new behaviors from the input sequence alone without any parameter updates. Recent studies have shown that ICL can surpass the original meaning learned in pretraining stage through internalizing the structure the data-generating process (DGP) of the prompt into the hidden representations. However, the mechanisms by which LLMs achieve this ability is left open. In this paper, we present the first rigorous explanation of such phenomena by introducing a unified framework of double convergence, where hidden representations converge both over context and across layers. This double convergence process leads to an implicit bias towards smooth (low-frequency) representations, which we prove analytically and verify empirically. Our theory explains several open empirical observations, including why learned representations exhibit globally structured but locally distorted geometry, and why their total energy decays without vanishing. Moreover, our theory predicts that ICL has an intrinsic robustness towards high-frequency noise, which we empirically confirm. These results provide new insights into the underlying mechanisms of ICL, and a theoretical foundation to study it that hopefully extends to more general data distributions and settings.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Evaluating Transformer's Ability to Learn Mildly Context-Sensitive Languages
papers.research_question: How well do Transformers learn mildly context-sensitive languages (MCSLs) from finite examples, in terms of generalizing to in-distribution data and extrapolating to longer strings? What kind of meaningful representations or patterns do the models learn?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically evaluates the Transformer's ability to learn a variety of mildly context-sensitive languages (MCSLs), finding that while they generalize well to in-distribution data, their ability to extrapolate to longer strings is worse than that of LSTMs. Analyses show the learned self-attention patterns model dependency relations and representations encode count information.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn mildly context-sensitive languages from finite examples and leverage self-attention to model dependency relations, but their extrapolation ability is limited compared to LSTMs. The learned patterns and behaviors provide insights into the models' linguistic capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers generalize well to unseen in-distribution data for MCSLs, performing comparably to LSTMs.
Transformers' ability to extrapolate to longer strings (out-of-distribution) is limited and generally worse than LSTMs.
Removing sinusoidal positional encoding in Transformer decoders (next character prediction tasks) can improve extrapolation ability.
Learned self-attention patterns often reflect the symbol dependency relations within the string (e.g., checkerboard patterns for crossing dependencies).
For the complex scramble language MIX, the learned representations encode count information for symbol occurrences, which may aid in solving the language.
papers.limitation:
The empirical study is bounded by a string length upper bound, so the dataset is bounded and might form a language with reduced complexity, weakening arguments about general learnability.
The roles of other heads, the feed-forward sublayer, etc. are not investigated, so it cannot be definitively said how self-attention directly contributed to inference.
papers.abstract: Despite the fact that Transformers perform well in NLP tasks, recent studies suggest that self-attention is theoretically limited in learning even some regular and context-free languages. These findings motivated us to think about their implications in modeling natural language, which is hypothesized to be mildly context-sensitive. We test the Transformer's ability to learn mildly context-sensitive languages of varying complexities, and find that they generalize well to unseen in-distribution data, but their ability to extrapolate to longer strings is worse than that of LSTMs. Our analyses show that the learned self-attention patterns and representations modeled dependency relations and demonstrated counting behavior, which may have helped the models solve the languages.

papers.title: A Review of Developmental Interpretability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is developmental interpretability, and how does it help understand the formation and evolution of capabilities in Large Language Models during training?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes the field of developmental interpretability for LLMs, highlighting how understanding training dynamics can provide insights into capability formation and enhance AI safety.
papers.conclusion: Developmental interpretability reveals LLMs as dynamic systems with rich ontogeny, providing a proactive approach to AI safety by understanding capability formation during training.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form through composition of attention heads, enabling in-context learning.
Knowledge acquisition follows a biphasic pattern from formation to optimization.
