Emergent abilities arise as phase transitions when pre-training loss crosses critical thresholds.
In-context learning can be transient and replaced by in-weights learning during overtraining.
Grokking involves delayed generalization after memorization.
papers.limitation:
Coverage limitations remain significant across current methodologies.
Feature ontology challenges include poorly defined concepts of what constitutes a 'feature'.
future_direction: Developing a unified theory of developmental dynamics
Creating robust benchmarks and metrics for interpretability
Expanding interpretability to multimodal and agentic AI systems
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the nascent but critical field of developmental interpretability for Large Language Models. We chart the field's evolution from static, post-hoc analysis of trained models to a dynamic investigation of the training process itself. We begin by surveying the foundational methodologies, including representational probing, causal tracing, and circuit analysis, that enable researchers to deconstruct the learning process. The core of this review examines the developmental arc of LLM capabilities, detailing key findings on the formation and composition of computational circuits, the biphasic nature of knowledge acquisition, the transient dynamics of learning strategies like in-context learning, and the phenomenon of emergent abilities as phase transitions in training. We explore illuminating parallels with human cognitive and linguistic development, which provide valuable conceptual frameworks for understanding LLM learning. Finally, we argue that this developmental perspective is not merely an academic exercise but a cornerstone of proactive AI safety, offering a pathway to predict, monitor, and align the processes by which models acquire their capabilities. We conclude by outlining the grand challenges facing the field, such as scalability and automation, and propose a research agenda for building more transparent, reliable, and beneficial AI systems.

papers.title: Complementary Explanations for Effective In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do explanations function in in-context learning, and what makes them effective?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an MMR-based exemplar selection method that improves in-context learning performance by selecting explanations that are both relevant and complementary.
papers.conclusion: The MMR-based exemplar selection strategy successfully improves in-context learning performance across three real-world tasks on multiple LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Both the computation trace and natural language in explanations contribute to their effectiveness in in-context learning.
LLMs can benefit from exemplar sets that exhibit complementarity and relevance to the test query.
The proposed MMR-based exemplar selection strategy, which balances relevance and diversity, outperforms nearest-neighbor selection.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to English datasets.
The MMR-based method requires pairwise similarity computation among exemplars, which can be costly when the pool is large.
Findings are based on a set of reasoning tasks and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Future work could explore extending the approach to multilingual settings and other task domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable capabilities in learning from expla- nations in prompts, but there has been limited understanding of exactly how these explana- tions function or why they are effective. This work aims to better understand the mechanisms by which explanations are used for in-context learning. We first study the impact of two dif- ferent factors on the performance of prompts with explanations: the computation trace (the way the solution is decomposed) and the natural language used to express the prompt. By per- turbing explanations on three controlled tasks, we show that both factors contribute to the ef- fectiveness of explanations. We further study how to form maximally effective sets of expla- nations for solving a given test query. We find that LLMs can benefit from the complemen- tarity of the explanation set: diverse reasoning skills shown by different exemplars can lead to better performance. Therefore, we propose a maximal marginal relevance-based exemplar selection approach for constructing exemplar sets that are both relevant as well as comple- mentary, which successfully improves the in- context learning performance across three real- world tasks on multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: How do Large Language Models Learn In-Context? Query and Key Matrices of In-Context Heads are Two Towers for Metric Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work in large language models, specifically for sentence classification with semantically-unrelated labels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a hypothesis that in-context heads use query and key matrices as two towers for metric learning, explaining the mechanism of in-context learning. Based on this, it introduces methods to reduce majority label bias and recency bias.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies in-context heads and proposes a hypothesis for ICL mechanism, providing insights into biases and methods to mitigate them.
papers.key_findings:
Intervening in only 1% of heads (in-context heads) significantly affects ICL accuracy from 87.6% to 24.4%.
Value-output vectors at label positions contain substantial information about the corresponding labels.
Prediction shifts are primarily due to changes in attention scores in in-context heads.
The hypothesis explains majority label bias and recency bias in ICL.
Proposed methods reduce majority label bias by 22% and recency bias by 17%.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on in-context heads in deep layers and does not fully explore how shallow layers transfer features into label positions.
The attribution methods used have limitations, and there is no unified method for attributing important modules.
future_direction: Explore other ICL tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
Design better attribution methods for identifying important modules.
Reduce recency bias during feature extraction in shallow layers.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) on sentence classification tasks with semantically-unrelated labels ("foo"/"bar"). We find intervening in only 1\% heads (named "in-context heads") significantly affects ICL accuracy from 87.6\% to 24.4\%. To understand this phenomenon, we analyze the value-output vectors in these heads and discover that the vectors at each label position contain substantial information about the corresponding labels. Furthermore, we observe that the prediction shift from "foo" to "bar" is due to the respective reduction and increase in these heads' attention scores at "foo" and "bar" positions. Therefore, we propose a hypothesis for ICL: in in-context heads, the value-output matrices extract label features, while the query-key matrices compute the similarity between the features at the last position and those at each label position. The query and key matrices can be considered as two towers that learn the similarity metric between the last position's features and each demonstration at label positions. Using this hypothesis, we explain the majority label bias and recency bias in ICL and propose two methods to reduce these biases by 22\% and 17\%, respectively.

papers.title: Repetitions are not all alike: distinct mechanisms sustain repetition in language models
papers.research_question: What are the distinct underlying mechanisms that sustain repetition in language models, and how do they develop during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that repetition in language models arises from two distinct mechanisms: a learned, circuit-based mechanism for in-context learning-induced repetition and an early-emerging, fallback mechanism for natural repetition.
papers.conclusion: Repetition in language models stems from two distinct mechanisms: a learned, circuit-based mechanism for ICL-induced repetition and an early-emerging fallback mechanism for natural repetition, which arises when the model fails to attend to informative tokens.
papers.key_findings:
ICL-induced repetition develops progressively over training, while natural repetition emerges early and persists.
ICL repetition relies on a dedicated circuit of attention heads that specialize over training, while natural repetition does not show such circuitry.
Attention during natural repetition focuses disproportionately on low-information tokens (like newlines), suggesting a fallback behavior.
MLP contributions to repetition are strong in ICL but weak in natural repetition.
ICL repetition leads to lower entropy (higher confidence) as cycles increase, while natural repetition shows higher uncertainty.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia, a relatively small-scale model, and may not generalize to other models or architectures.
future_direction: Extend analysis to models of varying sizes and architectures.
Investigate the causal mechanisms behind early-emerging repetition patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can sometimes degrade into repetitive loops, persistently generating identical word sequences. Because repetition is rare in natural human language, its frequent occurrence across diverse tasks and contexts in LLMs remains puzzling. Here we investigate whether behaviorally similar repetition patterns arise from distinct underlying mechanisms and how these mechanisms develop during model training. We contrast two conditions: repetitions elicited by natural text prompts with those induced by in-context learning (ICL) setups that explicitly require copying behavior. Our analyses reveal that ICL-induced repetition relies on a dedicated network of attention heads that progressively specialize over training, whereas naturally occurring repetition emerges early and lacks a defined circuitry. Attention inspection further shows that natural repetition focuses disproportionately on low-information tokens, suggesting a fallback behavior when relevant context cannot be retrieved. These results indicate that superficially similar repetition behaviors originate from qualitatively different internal processes, reflecting distinct modes of failure and adaptation in language models.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once: LLMs can In-Context Learn Multiple Tasks in Superposition
papers.research_question: Can LLMs perform multiple distinct in-context learning tasks simultaneously in a single inference call (task superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can perform multiple distinct in-context learning tasks simultaneously in a single inference call (task superposition), and this capability emerges even when trained on one task at a time.
papers.conclusion: Task superposition is the ability of LLMs to simultaneously solve distinct tasks from in-context examples, present in various pretrained models and improves with model size, with evidence that models internally mix task vectors.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can in-context learn multiple tasks in superposition when provided with prompts of a mixture of task examples.
Transformers can in-context learn multiple tasks in superposition even if trained to in-context learn one task at a time.
LLMs internally combine task vectors during task superposition.
Convex combinations of task vectors produce task superposition.
Larger models can solve more tasks in parallel and better calibrate their output distribution.
papers.limitation: Conventional decoding algorithms lead to generation collapse, limiting practical application of task superposition.
future_direction: Developing decoding strategies to maintain multi-task state throughout generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. In this study, we explore a surprising phenomenon related to ICL: LLMs can perform multiple, computationally distinct ICL tasks simultaneously, during a single inference call, a capability we term "task superposition". We provide empirical evidence of this phenomenon across various LLM families and scales and show that this phenomenon emerges even if we train the model to in-context learn one task at a time. We offer theoretical explanations that this capability is well within the expressive power of transformers. We also explore how LLMs internally compose task vectors during superposition. Furthermore, we show that larger models can solve more ICL tasks in parallel, and better calibrate their output distribution. Our findings offer insights into the latent capabilities of LLMs, further substantiate the perspective of "LLMs as superposition of simulators", and raise questions about the mechanisms enabling simultaneous task execution.

papers.title: What Can Transformers Learn In-Context? A Case Study of Simple Function Classes
papers.research_question: Can we train a model to in-context learn a function class? What is the relationship between tasks on which in-context learning succeeds and the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can be trained from scratch to perform in-context learning of simple function classes (e.g., linear functions) with performance comparable to optimal estimators, and this ability generalizes under distribution shifts and extends to more complex function classes.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can encode complex learning algorithms for in-context learning of various function classes, generalizing under distribution shifts, and this work lays groundwork for future research on in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can be trained to in-context learn linear functions with error comparable to the optimal least squares estimator.
The trained model generalizes to out-of-distribution prompts, including shifts in input distributions, label noise, and mismatches between in-context examples and query inputs.
Transformers can in-context learn more complex function classes (sparse linear functions, two-layer neural networks, decision trees) with performance matching or exceeding specialized algorithms like Lasso or gradient descent.
Model capacity and problem dimensionality affect in-context learning performance; larger models handle higher dimensions and distribution shifts better.
Curriculum learning drastically speeds up training without significantly affecting final performance.
papers.limitation:
Understanding the implications of these results for large language models requires further investigation.
Model performance degrades under some distribution shifts, e.g., with skewed covariance or extreme scaling of prompt inputs.
future_direction: Investigating the complexity of in-context learning in terms of function class, model capacity, and training data.
Understanding why curriculum learning speeds up training and whether similar speedups are possible for large language models.
Comparing inductive biases of different model families (e.g., Transformers vs. LSTMs) for in-context learning.
papers.abstract: In-context learning refers to the ability of a model to condition on a prompt sequence consisting of in-context examples (input-output pairs corresponding to some task) along with a new query input, and generate the corresponding output. Crucially, in-context learning happens only at inference time without any parameter updates to the model. While large language models such as GPT-3 exhibit some ability to perform in-context learning, it is unclear what the relationship is between tasks on which this succeeds and what is present in the training data. To make progress towards understanding in-context learning, we consider the well-defined problem of training a model to in-context learn a function class (e.g., linear functions): that is, given data derived from some functions in the class, can we train a model to in-context learn "most" functions from this class? We show empirically that standard Transformers can be trained from scratch to perform in-context learning of linear functions -- that is, the trained model is able to learn unseen linear functions from in-context examples with performance comparable to the optimal least squares estimator. In fact, in-context learning is possible even under two forms of distribution shift: (i) between the training data of the model and inference-time prompts, and (ii) between the in-context examples and the query input during inference. We also show that we can train Transformers to in-context learn more complex function classes -- namely sparse linear functions, two-layer neural networks, and decision trees -- with performance that matches or exceeds task-specific learning algorithms. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/dtsip/in-context-learning .

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: The representation landscape of few-shot learning and fine-tuning in large language models
papers.research_question: How do in-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) affect the geometry of the internal representations in large language models when solving the same question-answering task?
papers.core_contribution: ICL and SFT create very different internal representation structures in LLMs for the same task, with ICL forming semantically organized clusters in early layers and SFT forming sharper answer-encoding clusters in later layers.
papers.conclusion: Geometric analysis reveals a transition between layers encoding high-level semantic information and those generating answers, showing fine-tuning and few-shot learning take distinct approaches to extract information from LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Both few-shot learning and fine-tuning show a clear division between model layers, with a marked peak in intrinsic dimension and a sudden change in geometrical structure in the middle of the network.
Few-shot learning leads to semantically meaningful clustering of representations in early layers, organized hierarchically by subject.
Fine-tuning enhances the sharp emergence of clustered representations according to answer identity in the second half of the network.
The representation landscape of ICL is more interpretable in early layers, while SFT is fuzzier in early layers but develops better-defined answer-encoding peaks later.
The transition layer separates layers encoding high-level semantics from those involved in generating answers.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) are two common strategies for improving the performance of modern large language models (LLMs) on specific tasks. Despite their different natures, these strategies often lead to comparable performance gains. However, little is known about whether they induce similar representations inside LLMs. We approach this problem by analyzing the probability landscape of their hidden representations in the two cases. More specifically, we compare how LLMs solve the same question-answering task, finding that ICL and SFT create very different internal structures, in both cases undergoing a sharp transition in the middle of the network. In the first half of the network, ICL shapes interpretable representations hierarchically organized according to their semantic content. In contrast, the probability landscape obtained with SFT is fuzzier and semantically mixed. In the second half of the model, the fine-tuned representations develop probability modes that better encode the identity of answers, while the landscape of ICL representations is characterized by less defined peaks. Our approach reveals the diverse computational strategies developed inside LLMs to solve the same task across different conditions, allowing us to make a step towards designing optimal methods to extract information from language models.

papers.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
papers.research_question: How can in-context learning be made more effective and controllable through latent space steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes In-Context Vectors (ICV), an inference-only method that recasts in-context learning as latent space steering, making it more effective, controllable, and efficient than standard ICL and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ICV improves the effectiveness and efficiency of in-context learning, enabling LLMs to adapt to tasks without fine-tuning and combine multiple tasks through vector arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
ICV outperforms standard in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning on diverse tasks including language detoxification, style transfer, and role-playing.
The strength of ICV can be controlled by adjusting the scaling factor λ, allowing trade-offs between task adherence and semantic preservation.
ICV benefits from more demonstration examples, similar to ICL, but without context length constraints.
ICV is most effective when applied to all layers of the transformer, rather than individual layers.
ICV enables task arithmetic, allowing multiple tasks to be combined through vector addition and negation.
papers.limitation: ICV requires access to the model to add the in-context vector, which is easy for open-source models but may be a constraint for closed models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate emergent in-context learning capabilities, where they adapt to new tasks based on example demonstrations. However, in-context learning has seen limited effectiveness in many settings, is difficult to quantitatively control and takes up context window space. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative approach that recasts in-context learning as in-context vectors (ICV). Using ICV has two steps. We first use a forward pass on demonstration examples to create the in-context vector from the latent embedding of the LLM. This vector captures essential information about the intended task. On a new query, instead of adding demonstrations to the prompt, we shift the latent states of the LLM using the ICV. The ICV approach has several benefits: 1) it enables the LLM to more effectively follow the demonstration examples; 2) it's easy to control by adjusting the magnitude of the ICV; 3) it reduces the length of the prompt by removing the in-context demonstrations; 4) ICV is computationally much more efficient than fine-tuning. We demonstrate that ICV achieves better performance compared to standard in-context learning and fine-tuning on diverse tasks including safety, style transfer, role-playing and formatting. Moreover, we show that we can flexibly teach LLM to simultaneously follow different types of instructions by simple vector arithmetics on the corresponding ICVs.

papers.title: Analyzing the Structure of Attention in a Transformer Language Model
papers.research_question: Does attention align with syntactic dependency relations? Which attention heads attend to which part-of-speech tags? How does attention capture long-distance relationships versus short-distance ones?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes attention in the GPT-2 Transformer language model, finding that attention heads specialize in particular part-of-speech tags at different layers, attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in middle layers, and the deepest layers capture the most distant relationships.
papers.conclusion: The structure of attention in GPT-2 is closely tied to the language modeling objective, with attention patterns often focusing on words relevant for predicting the next token. The analysis provides human-interpretable descriptions of model behavior and is complementary to linguistic probing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model.
Attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers.
The deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships.
Attention heads exhibit specific patterns, such as focusing on acronyms, place names, or head nouns, as revealed by exemplar sentences.
Attention variability distinguishes content-dependent from content-independent (position-based) heads.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Wikipedia text, which has a specific encyclopedic format and style, so it is unclear how attention patterns manifest in other types of content.
Attention may not fully explain individual model predictions, as noted by recent work (Jain and Wallace, 2019).
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other Transformer models such as BERT, which has a bidirectional architecture and is trained on both token-level and sentence-level tasks.
Analyze attention patterns in other types of content, such as dialog scripts or song lyrics.
Analyze attention patterns in longer texts, especially for new Transformer variants like Transformer-XL and Sparse Transformer.
papers.abstract: The Transformer is a fully attention-based alternative to recurrent networks that has achieved state-of-the-art results across a range of NLP tasks. In this paper, we analyze the structure of attention in a Transformer language model, the GPT-2 small pretrained model. We visualize attention for individual instances and analyze the interaction between attention and syntax over a large corpus. We find that attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model, and that attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers. We also find that the deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships. Finally, we extract exemplar sentences that reveal highly specific patterns targeted by particular attention heads.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: When Parts Are Greater Than Sums: Individual LLM Components Can Outperform Full Models
papers.research_question: How do individual components (attention heads and MLPs) behave in in-context learning, and can they outperform the full model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that individual attention heads and MLPs can have higher accuracy than the full model in ICL, and proposes component reweighting, a method to learn to scale component contributions from few-shot examples, improving ICL accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The decomposition provides a new perspective on ICL, revealing consistent component characteristics, and motivates a practical method (component reweighting) that improves ICL accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Good-performing components exist that individually outperform the full model on classification tasks.
Bad-performing components perform below chance accuracy.
Label-biased components always predict the same label regardless of input.
Component accuracies are consistent across different demonstration sets and contrastive templates.
Component reweighting, which learns to scale component contributions from few labeled examples, improves ICL accuracy over standard ICL.
papers.limitation:
Component reweighting requires a small set of labeled data for training the weights.
The method is only experimented with classification tasks, leaving generation tasks for future work.
The paper does not focus on circuits, so mechanistic understanding of components is limited.
future_direction: Generalize the method to generation tasks.
papers.abstract: This paper studies in-context learning by decomposing the output of large language models into the individual contributions of attention heads and MLPs (components). We observe curious components: good-performing ones that individually do well on a classification task, even when the model performs poorly; bad-performing ones that do much worse than chance; and label-biased components that always predict the same label. We find that component accuracies are well-correlated across different demonstration sets and perturbations of prompt templates. Based on our findings, we propose component reweighting, which learns to linearly re-scale the component activations from a few labeled examples. Given 24 labeled examples, our method improves by an average of 6.0% accuracy points over 24-shot ICL across 8 tasks on Llama-2-7B. Overall, this paper both enriches our understanding of ICL and provides a practical method for improvement by examining model internals.

papers.title: Spin glass model of in-context learning
papers.research_question: What contributes to the emergence ability of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models, and how can it be explained mechanistically?
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps a linear attention transformer to a spin glass model, providing a statistical mechanics explanation for how task diversity during pre-training leads to the emergence of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The spin glass model offers a theoretical explanation for the emergence of in-context learning in transformers, linking it to statistical physics and providing insights into the intelligence boundary.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing task diversity leads to a unique ground state in the spin glass model, enabling in-context learning.
The model exhibits a phase transition to in-context learning as task diversity increases.
The approximate message passing (AMP) equations derived from the spin glass model match the results of stochastic gradient descent training.
The energy landscape has a single global minimum with high task diversity, but multiple local minima with low diversity.
future_direction: Explaining chain-of-thought prompting
Addressing hallucination
Extending to more complex transformers and tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models show a surprising in-context learning ability -- being able to use a prompt to form a prediction for a query, yet without additional training, in stark contrast to old-fashioned supervised learning. Providing a mechanistic interpretation and linking the empirical phenomenon to physics are thus challenging and remain unsolved. We study a simple yet expressive transformer with linear attention and map this structure to a spin glass model with real-valued spins, where the couplings and fields explain the intrinsic disorder in data. The spin glass model explains how the weight parameters interact with each other during pre-training, and further clarifies why an unseen function can be predicted by providing only a prompt yet without further training. Our theory reveals that for single-instance learning, increasing the task diversity leads to the emergence of in-context learning, by allowing the Boltzmann distribution to converge to a unique correct solution of weight parameters. Therefore the pre-trained transformer displays a prediction power in a novel prompt setting. The proposed analytically tractable model thus offers a promising avenue for thinking about how to interpret many intriguing but puzzling properties of large language models.

papers.title: CoT-ICL Lab: A Synthetic Framework for Studying Chain-of-Thought Learning from In-Context Demonstrations
papers.research_question: How do transformer models learn chain-of-thought reasoning in-context, and what factors (model size, number of in-context examples, etc.) facilitate this learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT-ICL Lab, a synthetic framework for generating tokenized datasets to systematically study chain-of-thought in-context learning, and provides empirical insights into how CoT accelerates learning and how model architecture and data complexity affect performance.
papers.conclusion: CoT-ICL Lab serves as a flexible and controllable framework for studying CoT-ICL, providing insights into the role of CoT for ICL that are important for understanding large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CoT accelerates the accuracy transition to higher values across model sizes during training.
Model depth is crucial for leveraging CoT with limited in-context examples, while more examples help shallow models match deeper model performance.
Limiting the diversity of token processing functions throughout training improves causal structure learning via ICL.
Embedding subspace similarity (sim(Edata, ETF)) correlates with transitions in evaluation accuracy.
When token processing functions are limited, the model's attention maps reflect the underlying causal DAG structure.
papers.limitation: The synthetic tokens in CoT-ICL Lab are not grounded in real-world concepts and do not capture the linguistic properties of natural language.
papers.abstract: We introduce CoT-ICL Lab, a framework and methodology to generate synthetic tokenized datasets and systematically study chain-of-thought (CoT) in-context learning (ICL) in language models. CoT-ICL Lab allows fine grained control over the complexity of in-context examples by decoupling (1) the causal structure involved in chain token generation from (2) the underlying token processing functions. We train decoder-only transformers (up to 700M parameters) on these datasets and show that CoT accelerates the accuracy transition to higher values across model sizes. In particular, we find that model depth is crucial for leveraging CoT with limited in-context examples, while more examples help shallow models match deeper model performance. Additionally, limiting the diversity of token processing functions throughout training improves causal structure learning via ICL. We also interpret these transitions by analyzing transformer embeddings and attention maps. Overall, CoT-ICL Lab serves as a simple yet powerful testbed for theoretical and empirical insights into ICL and CoT in language models.

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: Towards Understanding How Transformers Learn In-context Through a Representation Learning Lens
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) in Transformers work? Can ICL be related to gradient descent under the softmax attention setting without specific constructions for model weights and input tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the ICL inference process of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to gradient descent on a dual model, provides a representation learning interpretation, derives a generalization bound, and proposes attention modifications inspired by contrastive learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that ICL can be understood as gradient descent on a dual model from a representation learning perspective, and that attention modifications inspired by this view show promise in enhancing model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The ICL inference of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to one step of gradient descent on a dual model with a loss function that maximizes similarity between value-projected and key-projected tokens.
The dual model's training resembles a self-supervised representation learning process, analogous to contrastive learning without negative samples.
A generalization error bound for ICL is derived, showing the error decreases with the number of demonstration tokens.
The equivalence extends to a full Transformer layer (with FFN) and multiple attention layers.
Attention modifications inspired by representation learning (regularization, data augmentation, negative samples) can improve model performance on synthetic and GLUE tasks.
papers.limitation:
The negative sample selection method is too coarse and not always effective.
The attention modifications are tested on limited tasks and may not generalize.
future_direction: Develop more task-specific augmentation strategies for attention.
Design more effective methods for constructing negative samples in the attention mechanism.
Apply the representation learning lens to other model components and settings.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models based on Transformers have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities. With just a few demonstration examples, the models can implement new tasks without any parameter updates. However, it is still an open question to understand the mechanism of ICL. In this paper, we attempt to explore the ICL process in Transformers through a lens of representation learning. Initially, leveraging kernel methods, we figure out a dual model for one softmax attention layer. The ICL inference process of the attention layer aligns with the training procedure of its dual model, generating token representation predictions that are equivalent to the dual model's test outputs. We delve into the training process of this dual model from a representation learning standpoint and further derive a generalization error bound related to the quantity of demonstration tokens. Subsequently, we extend our theoretical conclusions to more complicated scenarios, including one Transformer layer and multiple attention layers. Furthermore, drawing inspiration from existing representation learning methods especially contrastive learning, we propose potential modifications for the attention layer. Finally, experiments are designed to support our findings.

papers.title: Next-token pretraining implies in-context learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning emerge as a necessary consequence of next-token pretraining, rather than being an exotic emergent property?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning is a mathematically inevitable consequence of optimizing next-token prediction objectives, and provides an information-theoretic framework to predict ICL dynamics for correlated stochastic processes.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is a natural, predictable outcome of next-token pretraining, grounded in architecture- and modality-independent information-theoretic principles.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning necessarily arises from next-token pretraining on correlated sequences, rather than being an exotic emergent property.
The reduction of in-context loss (predictive uncertainty) with more context can be precisely predicted using the mixed-state presentation (MSP) of the data-generating process.
Induction heads are a useful mechanism for disambiguating between different ergodic components in non-ergodic training data.
Power-law decay of in-context loss emerges when training on non-ergodic processes or processes with hierarchical correlational structure.
A model's in-context performance on a specific task is mathematically coupled to the entire ensemble of tasks encountered during pretraining.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to in-distribution ICL; a full account of out-of-distribution ICL is beyond the current scope.
papers.abstract: We argue that in-context learning (ICL) predictably arises from standard self-supervised next-token pretraining, rather than being an exotic emergent property. This work establishes the foundational principles of this emergence by focusing on in-distribution ICL, demonstrating how models necessarily adapt to context when trained on token sequences, especially from non-ergodic sources. Our information-theoretic framework precisely predicts these in-distribution ICL dynamics (i.e., context-dependent loss reduction). We verify this with experiments using synthetic datasets of differing types of correlational structure, reproducing characteristic phenomena like phase transitions in training loss for induction head formation and power-law scaling of in-context loss. We further show that a model's in-context performance on any task is mathematically coupled to the ensemble of tasks seen in pretraining, offering a fundamental explanation, grounded in architecture- and modality-independent principles, for such inference-time learning.

papers.title: Rethinking Associative Memory Mechanism in Induction Head
papers.research_question: How does a two-layer transformer capture in-context information and balance it with pretrained bigram knowledge in next token prediction, from the viewpoint of associative memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows theoretically and empirically that relative positional encoding enables two-layer transformers to avoid oversight of patterns in long sequences and investigates how the model balances in-context knowledge with global knowledge during next token prediction.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes the interaction between global bigram and in-context knowledge in two-layer transformers through associative memory, showing that RPE empowers transformers to capture information in longer sequences and explaining how next token prediction balances different knowledge sources.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers with relative positional encoding (RPE) can attend to previous tokens regardless of position, while those with absolute positional encoding (APE) fail for later positions.
The model's output logits depend on both global knowledge (bigram statistics) and the frequency of token patterns in the context.
A three-layer transformer without any positional encoding can implement the induction head mechanism.
The induction head mechanism can be understood as an associative memory that stores associations between tokens and their contexts.
papers.limitation: If the input sequence contains out-of-distribution tokens, the induction head mechanism does not activate for transformers with RPE, whereas transformers with APE can still attend to the previous token.
papers.abstract: Induction head mechanism is a part of the computational circuits for in-context learning (ICL) that enable large language models (LLMs) to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning. Most existing work explains the training dynamics behind acquiring such a powerful mechanism. However, the model's ability to coordinate in-context information over long contexts and global knowledge acquired during pretraining remains poorly understood. This paper investigates how a two-layer transformer thoroughly captures in-context information and balances it with pretrained bigram knowledge in next token prediction, from the viewpoint of associative memory. We theoretically analyze the representation of weight matrices in attention layers and the resulting logits when a transformer is given prompts generated by a bigram model. In the experiments, we design specific prompts to evaluate whether the outputs of the trained transformer align with the theoretical results.

papers.title: UniBias: Unveiling and Mitigating LLM Bias through Internal Attention and FFN Manipulation
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms within LLMs that cause bias, and can we identify and mitigate these biased components to improve in-context learning performance and robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces UniBias, an inference-only method that identifies and eliminates biased FFN vectors and attention heads in LLMs by projecting internal components to vocabulary space and applying three criteria, leading to improved ICL performance and reduced prompt brittleness.
papers.conclusion: UniBias effectively mitigates LLM bias by manipulating internal structures, achieving state-of-the-art ICL performance and enhancing robustness against prompt brittleness.
papers.key_findings:
FFN vectors and attention heads are internal components that contribute to various bias factors like vanilla label bias, recency bias, and selection bias.
UniBias identifies biased components using three criteria: relatedness to label prediction, biased logit distribution, and low variance across samples.
UniBias significantly improves ICL performance across 12 NLP datasets and multiple model sizes (Llama-2 7B/13B, GPT-J, GPT2-XL), outperforming existing calibration methods.
UniBias alleviates prompt brittleness, making model performance more stable under changes in example selection, order, and prompt formatting.
Some biased components are shared across tasks, suggesting the potential for identifying global biased components for cross-task bias mitigation.
papers.limitation: The method relies on grid searching with a small set of labeled training samples.
future_direction: Reduce reliance on labeled samples for grid searching to improve efficiency and applicability.
Identify global biased components that mitigate bias across multiple tasks and diverse prompt settings.
Use identified biased components as sensors for guiding effective prompt generation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various tasks using the in-context learning (ICL) paradigm. However, their effectiveness is often compromised by inherent bias, leading to prompt brittleness, i.e., sensitivity to design settings such as example selection, order, and prompt formatting. Previous studies have addressed LLM bias through external adjustment of model outputs, but the internal mechanisms that lead to such bias remain unexplored. Our work delves into these mechanisms, particularly investigating how feedforward neural networks (FFNs) and attention heads result in the bias of LLMs. By Interpreting the contribution of individual FFN vectors and attention heads, we identify the biased LLM components that skew LLMs' prediction toward specific labels. To mitigate these biases, we introduce UniBias, an inference-only method that effectively identifies and eliminates biased FFN vectors and attention heads. Extensive experiments across 12 NLP datasets demonstrate that UniBias significantly enhances ICL performance and alleviates prompt brittleness of LLMs.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Composition, Attention, or Both?
papers.research_question: Whether the composition function and the self-attention mechanism can both induce human-like syntactic generalization in language models.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Composition Attention Grammars (CAGs), a novel architecture that combines a recursive composition function and a self-attention mechanism, and demonstrates that both components are important for inducing human-like syntactic generalization in language models.
papers.conclusion: The composition function and the self-attention mechanism both play an important role in making language models more human-like in their syntactic generalization, with the composition function specifically allowing syntactic features to percolate into subtree representations.
papers.key_findings:
CAGs achieved the highest overall accuracy on the SyntaxGym benchmark, outperforming even GPT-2 trained on 250x more data with a 7x larger model size.
Explicit syntactic supervision (+Syntax) consistently improved both overall accuracy and perplexity across model types.
The composition function (+Composition) improved syntactic generalization performance, suggesting it allows syntactic features (but not semantic features) to percolate into subtree representations.
The self-attention mechanism (+SelfAttn) improved performance only when combined with explicit syntactic supervision, highlighting the importance of attending to previous structural information, not just words.
A dissociation was observed between perplexity and human-like syntactic generalization performance among syntactic language models.
papers.limitation: CAGs have a high computational cost due to recursive training and the memory consumption of the self-attention mechanism, making it difficult to train larger models.
future_direction: Introduce a computationally efficient self-attention mechanism to CAGs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel architecture called Composition Attention Grammars (CAGs) that recursively compose subtrees into a single vector representation with a composition function, and selectively attend to previous structural information with a self-attention mechanism. We investigate whether these components—the composition function and the self-attention mechanism—can both induce human-like syntactic generalization. Specifically, we train language models (LMs) with and without these two components with the model sizes carefully controlled, and evaluate their syntactic generalization performance against six test circuits on the SyntaxGym benchmark. The results demonstrated that the composition function and the self-attention mechanism both play an important role to make LMs more human-like, and closer inspection of linguistic phenomenon implied that the composition function allowed syntactic features, but not semantic features, to percolate into subtree representations.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Learning to grok: Emergence of in-context learning and skill composition in modular arithmetic tasks
papers.research_question: How do in-context learning and skill composition emerge in transformers trained on modular arithmetic tasks, and what are the conditions for out-of-distribution generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn to perform out-of-distribution generalization on modular arithmetic tasks through in-context learning and skill composition, with this ability emerging as the number of pre-training tasks increases and requiring early stopping in deeper models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to compose skills and perform out-of-distribution generalization on modular arithmetic tasks, with the emergence of this ability driven by the diversity of pre-training tasks and model depth.
papers.key_findings:
The model exhibits a transition from in-distribution to out-of-distribution generalization as the number of pre-training tasks increases.
The smallest model capable of out-of-distribution generalization requires two transformer blocks, and for deeper models, the generalization phase is transient and requires early stopping.
The model develops highly structured representations in attention heads and MLPs, which enable the implementation of algorithms like Ratio Matching and Modular Regression.
Deeper models (4-block) show an algorithmic shift from Ratio Matching to Modular Regression as the number of in-context examples increases, while shallower models (2-block) do not.
The model's ability to generalize out-of-distribution is determined by the number of pre-training tasks and the fraction of examples per task.
papers.abstract: Large language models can solve tasks that were not present in the training set. This capability is believed to be due to in-context learning and skill composition. In this work, we study the emergence of in-context learning and skill composition in a collection of modular arithmetic tasks. Specifically, we consider a finite collection of linear modular functions $z = a \, x + b \, y \;\mathrm{mod}\; p$ labeled by the vector $(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}_p^2$. We use some of these tasks for pre-training and the rest for out-of-distribution testing. We empirically show that a GPT-style transformer exhibits a transition from in-distribution to out-of-distribution generalization as the number of pre-training tasks increases. We find that the smallest model capable of out-of-distribution generalization requires two transformer blocks, while for deeper models, the out-of-distribution generalization phase is \emph{transient}, necessitating early stopping. Finally, we perform an interpretability study of the pre-trained models, revealing highly structured representations in both attention heads and MLPs; and discuss the learned algorithms. Notably, we find an algorithmic shift in deeper models, as we go from few to many in-context examples.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Language Models "Grok" to Copy
papers.research_question: How do language models develop context copying abilities during pre-training, and is this process similar to grokking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that language models develop context copying abilities through a process similar to grokking, with evidence from pre-training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The development of context copying in language models is a form of grokking, offering insights for improving language model training and in-context performance.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training loss decreases rapidly while context copying ability lags and then abruptly saturates, resembling grokking.
The development of copying ability is independent of the number of tokens trained, similar to grokking speed.
Induction heads form from shallow to deep layers during training, mirroring circuit development in grokking.
Regularization techniques like dropout and weight decay can accelerate or enhance the development of context copying.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on copying tasks and does not evaluate in-context learning (ICL) tasks, which are more complex, due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Applying the understanding of grokking to improve in-context capacities like ICL in language models.
papers.abstract: We examine the pre-training dynamics of language models, focusing on their ability to copy text from preceding context--a fundamental skill for various LLM applications, including in-context learning (ICL) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We propose a novel perspective that Transformer-based language models develop copying abilities similarly to grokking, which refers to sudden generalization on test set long after the model fit to the training set. Our experiments yield three arguments: (1) The pre-training loss decreases rapidly, while the context copying ability of models initially lags and then abruptly saturates. (2) The speed of developing copying ability is independent of the number of tokens trained, similarly to how grokking speed is unaffected by dataset size as long as the data distribution is preserved. (3) Induction heads, the attention heads responsible for copying, form from shallow to deep layers during training, mirroring the development of circuits in deeper layers during grokking. We contend that the connection between grokking and context copying can provide valuable insights for more effective language model training, ultimately improving in-context performance. For example, we demonstrated that techniques that enhance grokking, such as regularization, either accelerate or enhance the development of context copying.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
